articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Acquires Youngstown Flats, Adding 193 Homes to Portfolio
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Tuesday, the Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD) announced it is acquiring Youngstown Flats, a six-story apartment complex with 193 homes, located in West Seattle.

The property marks the recently funded public developer's second acquisition of an apartment complex. The SSHD's board granted a stamp of approval for the acquisition on Tuesday night. SSHD says it expects to buy Youngstown Flats for about $68 million and close on the property in mid-December.
Acquired at a cost of just over $352,000 per apartment, the Youngstown Flats is significantly cheaper than building a comparable housing complex from scratch.

With the addition of Youngstown Flats, SSHD will own a total of 343 units. In May, the developer announced its first purchase : Elara at the Market, a 150-unit complex near Pike Place Market. That 2018 building was slightly newer, but in the same general age range that the developer appears to be targeting in its early acquisitions.

Earlier this month, SSHD announced its first construction project in the Central District, aiming to add 20 homes on a 7,000-square-foot lot donated by the family of former House Speaker Frank Chopp, who passed away in 2025 after a long career as a champion for affordable housing at the state legislature. As a new construction project still in the design phase, those units will take longer to come online but are expected to open in 2028.

Youngtown Flats includes a broad range of unit sizes, which the SSHD pointed to as a selling point: "One of the central attractions of the complex were its large unit sizes. On average, each apartment is more than 800 square feet, and Youngstown Flats offers nearly 50 two-bedroom apartments." More recent apartment developments have tended to focus on one-bedroom units and to spurn multi-bedrooms, given current market realities.

“This is a tremendous opportunity for SSHD,” said the agency’s interim CEO Tiffani McCoy in a statement. “Providing permanently affordable, family-sized housing in different parts of Seattle is what we’re all about.”

Located at 4040 26th Ave SW, Youngstown Flats was developed by Barrientos Ryan and Legacy Partners. While a market-rate private development, the building participated in Seattle's Multifamily Tax Exemption (MFTE) program, which provided discounted rents to 20% of tenants in exchange for a property tax break. Since the building just passed the 12-year mark, SSHD noted it had aged out of MFTE, which was leading to rent pressure on residents in the formerly rent-restricted discounted units as the program lapsed.

"SSHD’s new ownership will potentially protect about 30 residents from economic displacement by offering them a permanent affordability program under the social housing model," the agency noted in a press release.

Excellent transit access was another attribute that SSHD underscored, pointing to two convenient nearby RapidRide bus lines: the H Line and C Line. The complex will also be a short walk from the Delridge light rail station planned as part of Sound Transit's planned West Seattle Link Extension, which will add 3.9 miles of service from SoDo to Alaska Junction in 2035 (following a series of planning delays) .

Given worries that light rail's arrival may drive up rents and displacement pressure on existing residents, social housing could provide an antidote to that dynamic, sheltering some housing stock from the whims of the market.

The complex is near the northern stub of the Longfellow Creek Legacy Trail, a hiking path through a greenbelt disrupted by West Seattle Golf Course, but continuing farther south. The Nucor steel mill is a few blocks north of the property, and a state driver's licensing office is next door.
Seattle Councilmember Rob Saka, who represents District 1 including West Seattle, celebrated the acquisition.

“I am so happy to see social housing being built in my district. Mixed-income communities, where those at lower incomes pay less in rent than those who make more, is an effective way of addressing Seattle’s housing and affordability crisis," Saka said in a statement. "And with transit-oriented development, residents can more easily reach work, school, and essential services.”

In 2024, Saka joined the centrist council majority in voting to put a competing measure on the ballot , which had the intent of blocking the excess compensation tax that will ultimately fund the Youngstown Flats acquisition and SSHD's other additions. Seattle voters ultimately rejected that council alternative and approved the grassroots "Prop 1A" measure in February 2025 – even in the face of opposition from then-Mayor Bruce Harrell and the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce.
The high earners tax that Proposition 1A set in motion pulled in more revenue than expected, netting $115 million in its first year. That funding is what is powering the SSHD's buying spree.

Eventually, the SSHD plans to shift its focus to constructing new housing, rather than procuring existing apartment complexes. To get started, the acquisition strategy allows the SSHD to grow its portfolio quickly and establish collateral for loans to fund future construction projects.

Tenants at the Youngstown Flats may not notice a huge difference immediately, but they will have greater certainty their rents will not spike unexpectedly and the agency is planning some perks that market-rate landlords do not typically offer. Among them: free, one-year ORCA transit passes to all residents.

"We also plan to get rid of junk fees and freeze rents for existing leases for two years, through December 2028," the agency said. "Though not immediate, over the course of the first year of our ownership, SSHD will end Ratio Utility Billing System (RUBS) charges at the property, saving residents on utility costs as well."

The Youngstown Flats acquisition will allow the SSHD to exceeding its housing pipeline goal for 2026, the agency said, adding it expects to unveil additional acquisitions next year. By the end of 2027, SSHD expects to own more than 1,000 units of housing, meaning it expects to add at least 650 homes to its social housing rolls next year.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Rich Conservatives Are Trying to Buy Washington’s Supreme Court Again, Don’t Let Them
articles.author: Austin Field
paras: In 2024, wealthy conservative political operatives tried to use dark money to install their handpicked candidate, Dave Larson, on Washington state’s Supreme Court. This year, those same wealthy conservatives are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars backing five state Supreme Court candidates, all of whom are also endorsed by the Washington Republican Party: Judge Sean O’Donnell, Scott Edwards, Judge David Stevens, Dave Larson, and Todd Bloom. Don’t let the wealthy buy Washington’s highest court.

Of these dark-money candidates, Judge O’Donnell seems to have the best shot at winning — despite his strong ties to Washington Republicans. He began his career as an aide to Republican Senator Slade Gorton, a staunch income tax opponent . The two remained close, Judge O’Donnell even led a prayer at Gorton’s funeral. Former Republican Attorney General Rob McKenna, another Gorton protégé , is also supporting Judge O’Donnell.

Powerful corporate interests are backing Judge O’Donnell, too. He’s raised $493,769.68 from donors like David Zapolsky, a top Amazon executive who led the effort to crush a warehouse unionization drive in Staten Island, and Bruce McCaw, a telecommunications heir who generously donates his ample inheritance to Republicans .

Judge O’Donnell is also benefitting from a $476,000 independent expenditure campaign primarily supported by three organizations. Balance Washington , funded by a wealthy millionaires’ tax opponent , has kicked in about $88,000. Citizens for Working Courts – funded by “Jobs PAC” which is backed by , among others, oil companies, tobacco companies, and Amazon — has contributed about $294,000.

Meanwhile, Concerned Taxpayers of Washington State — funded by prominent local Republicans including Brian Heywood , a prominent Trump donor who’s leading the fight against the millionaire’s tax and trans kids, and Steve Gordon, one of Washington’s top donors to Trump’s inaugural fund — has spent over $100,000 supporting Judge O’Donnell.

Judge O’Donnell’s opponent, Judge Ian Birk ( endorsed by The Urbanist Elections Committee, on which I serve) has raised reasonable questions about Judge O’Donnell’s deep personal, political, and financial ties to wealthy local conservatives — prompting a furious and misleading rebuke from the Seattle Times Editorial Board. After Judge Birk released a fundraising email pointing out Judge O’Donnell’s Republican affiliations, the Times accused Judge Birk of unethical “ gutter ” campaigning.

The Times later expressed alarm that Judge Birk was receiving support from a political action committee funded by “public sector unions, a personal injury firm, and an attorney for a personal injury firm.” The Times was particularly angry about Judge Birk’s support from personal injury attorneys, who successfully sued the State for $614 million last year, insinuating that their support for Judge Birk represented a conflict of interest. Overall, the Editorial Board groused, “Birk has all but stamped a blue “D” on his forehead.”

The Board’s misleading arguments make little sense. By their own logic, if Judge Birk — a widely respected jurist who boasts endorsements across the ideological spectrum — has a “D” on his forehead, then Judge O’Donnell has amply earned an “R” on his. And by relentlessly focusing on Judge Birk’s campaign donors while ignoring Judge O’Donnell’s massive cash infusions from wealthy conservatives, the Times Editorial Board could be credibly accused of the same “gutter” politics they claim to abhor.

Further, the Times’ attack on personal injury attorneys is an attack on the rule of law itself. Wealthy conservatives have disparaged personal injury attorneys for decades because they provide legal services to working people. The vast majority of Americans cannot afford lawyers. 51% can't afford healthcare . Personal injury attorneys, who typically do not charge unless their client receives a settlement or a favorable verdict, are some of the few private attorneys who represent vulnerable clients.

For example, those $614 million in legal settlements the Board is so mad about? 80% of those costs come from claims against Washington’s Department of Children, Youth, and Families, which oversees foster care and juvenile detention. DCYF has been battered by accusations that department staff were complicit in hundreds of cases of sexual abuse and neglect , a scandal rivalling those of the Catholic Church and the Boy Scouts. The Times Editorial Board — which has consistently supported youth incarceration — should be less concerned about the cost of those lawsuits, or the lawyers supporting Judge Birk, and more concerned with justice for abused children.

The Editorial Board is right about one thing, though: Washington’s courts should be fair and apolitical. But electing a Supreme Court justice with deep ties to Trump donors and powerful corporations will not depoliticize the Court.

The only way to depoliticize Washington’s courts is to return control over tax policy to the legislature. In 1933, five Washington Supreme Court justices seized control of taxation, delivering a political win for their wealthy supporters by overturning a popular income tax. That initial political decision created an unjust, unpredictable tax system and subsequently forced the Court to intervene in everything from school policy to capital gains taxation .

Depoliticizing the Court, then, requires returning political decisions, like taxation, to the politicians in the Legislature. We don’t know if Judge Birk will do that, but we can be reasonably sure, given his history and his connections, that Judge O’Donnell won’t. Don’t vote for Judge O’Donnell or the rest of the conservative dark-money slate.
Austin Field is an attorney and the Election Chair for the public defense chapter of SEIU 925. The views expressed are not those of his employer.

articles.title: Fight Over Traffic Safety in Seattle's Historic Districts Keeps Simmering
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: At a special meeting Monday, the Seattle City Council unanimously approved two pieces of legislation targeting the issue of traffic safety, but transportation committee chair Rob Saka's "SAFER Streets Act" package remains incomplete. A third bill, targeting the authority of officials at the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) to make upgrades relating to safety, remains in limbo.

Council Bill 121296 had been a fairly innocuous proposal until an amendment from Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck turned it into a lightning rod . Amendment 16, approved on a 3-2 committee vote last month, added a provision allowing Seattle's City Traffic Engineer to make certain changes within the city's historic districts without approval of the boards that oversee those districts.

If approved, adjustments that include "traffic control devices and spot design changes" would be exempt from landmark designation, and SDOT would be able to construct "traffic control devices" in historic districts without needing a certificate of approval, which is appealable. The change has been praised by traffic safety advocates, but the amendment quickly drew push back from preservation advocates, including members of the historic district boards themselves.

But CB 121296 doesn't appear to be in limbo because it lacks the vote to pass; despite the compressed timeline to consider amendments ahead of the committee vote, amendment 16 required additional analysis under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) given its scope. With that review expected to take several months, some councilmembers have reportedly pushed for an earlier vote that would be paired with another amendment entirely nullifying Amendment 16, but that hasn't occurred.

"We're working through, there's some legal challenges, legal concerns," Saka told The Urbanist at a press conference Monday, ahead of the vote on the other two SAFER Streets Act bills. "We're we're hoping to resolve that with that third bill, which is why we're we're not ready to vote on it today."
Though Saka cited a potential vote on November 10, that decision ultimately rests with Council President Joy Hollingsworth.

As it stands today, the approval process to make street upgrades in Seattle's eight historic districts provides leverage to slow and stymie those changes that simply doesn't exist in other neighborhoods. Though the adjustment would not give SDOT carte blanche to implement transportation changes in those districts – bollard installation wouldn't be covered under the amendment, for example – targeted upgrades related to safety would be able to be put on an expedited track.

One recent incident is taking center stage in the discussion around Amendment 16. Earlier this year, SDOT presented a proposal to add on-street bike and scooter corrals to 21 intersections across Pioneer Square, providing space for parking off the sidewalk in a way that also improves intersection visibility. With seven more on sidewalks, the corrals would have provided parking for around 300 bikes and scooters while only eliminating one or two legal parking spaces.

But business owners around the neighborhood came out to oppose the plan, with the advocacy group Alliance for Pioneer Square contending that the proposed design was "fundamentally misaligned with the character and the knowledge of the neighborhood." The group has argued Pioneer Square needs custom (higher cost) bike racks designed to look vintage, but also questioned the need for more racks and intersection daylighting.
Several months later, on the eve of being able to install the corrals in advance of the World Cup, SDOT returned with a proposal that only added three on-street corrals .
On October 14, the Pioneer Square Preservation District Board approved a motion to write a letter officially opposing the amendment, following a discussion on specific concerns.

"When everyone was concerned about the 30 corrals that were coming to the neighborhood, I think we wanted to slow SDOT down and ask them to get community feedback, and that process was great," said preservation board member Henry Watson, Development Manager at Urban Villages, which owns the RailSpur development. "A lot of business owners showed up. A lot of people who were concerned, and I think we got a lot better outcomes."

On the other end of downtown, the Pike Place Market Historical Commission is set to formally weigh in on Amendment 16 at a meeting later this week. The advocacy group Friends of the Market, which dates to 1964 and was formed to prevent the Market's demolition, has come out opposed to the change.

"The defining issue of Amendment 16 is not safety, which everyone can support. The issue is how to make decisions that promote safety while still respecting the protections afforded to special places by the careful judgments of the Boards and Commissions tasked with overseeing changes to the public spaces they know best," Friends board member Christine Vaughn wrote in the group's monthly newsletter. "Preservation and safety concerns can work hand-in-hand when Commissioners and SDOT collaborate to find solutions that fit within each district, but also meet the needs of traffic safety."
Maureen Elenga, an architectural historian and chair of the Pioneer Square board, portrayed supporters of Amendment 16 as being misinformed about the process to approve changes in historic districts.

"This is a group of people [who] complained to the city councilperson that special review districts aren't concerned with pedestrian safety, and they responded with this, which is, I think, not the appropriate way to conduct city policy," Elenga said. "We all know that that's not what happened. What happened was the process that is designed to happen. And if they if they want to come to us and discuss certain things that could be done administratively, sure, we can have that discussion. But just this wholesale trying to just remove our purview to review the right-of-way is not appropriate."

And yet, the proponents of the change include traffic safety advocates who have followed SDOT's process to implement projects for years, and are deeply familiar with the way that changes to streets within historic districts get approved... or delayed.

"If you're walking downtown on First Avenue headed south, the person with the ultimate responsibility for whether you're safe or not is [City Traffic Engineer] Venu Nemani, until you hit Columbia, and all of a sudden it becomes a preservation board," Gordon Padelford, Executive Director of the Seattle Streets Alliance, told councilmembers ahead of the committee vote on Amendment 16. "And that doesn't quite sit right when we're talking about public accountability, we're thinking about public safety. There needs to be someone with authority to make sure that our streets are safe."

Even if CB 121296 makes it across the finish line with Amendment 16 intact, the tension between the goals of the preservation boards and broader city aims around improving safety and mobility is definitely not going away.

"One of the things that everyone loves about Pioneer Square is how pedestrianized it is. It feels safe. It's great. This board is not against any of that. I think that's why everyone loves Pioneer Square," Watson said. "But I think the purpose of these discussions is to slow these things down."

articles.title: Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle startup Ganaz , which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn , saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million , with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award . “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”
At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

articles.title: F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s . Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.
F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.
F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.
The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool . Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”
We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI . Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.
This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

articles.title: PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based firm that specializes in selling intellectual property and other assets, announced this week that it’s been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time . Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020 . The founders were let go after the receivership , according to the site.
When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.
He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

articles.title: Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.
Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan .

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”
T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.
Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.
Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

articles.title: Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3 , was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.
Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release .
With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.
“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.
Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

articles.title: Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.
One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.
CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”
Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.
Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.
Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.
“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.
Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.
Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday . Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday . On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter .
Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

articles.title: Capitol Hill volunteers push for dedicated day shelter — and someone to take the lead
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A grassroots group of organizers pushing for a day shelter facility on Capitol Hill are looking to hand off and expand the effort.

“Even if you go to a night shelter, you have to leave at 6 or 7 in the morning — so you’re out there the rest of the time,” Lucia Sommers tells CHS. “Places like this do exist in Seattle. They’re just not on Capitol Hill.

The neighborhood group is holding a meeting on Monday, November 2, to address what they say is a critical gap in local social support and the lack of a daytime drop-in space for unsheltered residents where people can escape harsh weather, sit down, get water, use a restroom, and temporarily store their things.

To call Sommers and her fellow organizers a group is overstating things a bit. Sommers, who moved to Seattle a few years back after her husband passed away and she left San Francisco for the Pacific Northwest, said the Capitol Hill day shelter effort is led by a trio of volunteers who met through their work shifts helping at the Community Lunch on Capitol Hill meal program.

“I lived in San Francisco for 50 years and was involved very heavily with an organization that ran thee day shelters,” Sommers said. “I came here and the only thing I could find near my home was a lunch program.”
Sommers says Community Lunch’s work remains vital. A Capitol Hill day shelter would also meet important needs.

Sommers has since moved to Belltown and she says the others helping her organize around a new day shelter in Capitol Hill join her in seeing the need for a larger, broader push to create a facility. They’re hoping Monday’s meeting and the discussion can be the start of a hand-off.

The effort comes amid a surge in support and spending in Seattle for more long-term shelters that include beds as officials have embraced resources like tiny house villages as a vital component of reducing the homelessness crisis by establishing living spaces where people can also be connected to addiction, health, and housing resources.

The city and regional officials also continue to back overnight congregate shelters operated by nonprofit partners including Downtown Emergency Service Center, Compass Housing Alliance, and the Salvation Army.

Unlike overnight shelters that require guests to leave early in the morning, a day shelter operates to fulfill essential daily living needs. They don’t necessarily need to be focused on daytime hours. These centers can offer individuals a refuge from extreme cold, summer heat, and heavy rain. Beyond offering a place to sit, day centers can furnish basic sanitation facilities, drinking water, phone charging stations, and a mailing address, serving as a stable daytime anchor for people navigating life without permanent housing.

In Seattle and across King County, the day shelter model already plays a vital role in neighborhood stability. Programs such as the Urban Rest Stop in downtown Seattle and Ballard provide free access to restrooms, showers, and laundry machines. Similarly, Pioneer Square’s Compass Center Day Center serves as a daytime refuge where visitors can access warm meals, rest, and connect directly with housing counselors and case managers.

Across the country, cities from Portland to Denver and Boston have increasingly invested in dedicated daytime service hubs. In cities like Portland, centers such as the Blanchet House and Transition Projects provide daytime safety, meals, and clean clothing to hundreds of people each afternoon.

Urban planning and public health experts say that day centers reduce strain on public libraries, transit stations, and storefronts, offering structured support rather than leaving vulnerable people to wander neighborhood commercial corridors during business hours.
There is nothing like that currently operating on Capitol Hill, Sommers said.

Organizers of the Capitol Hill meeting say that finding an effective neighborhood solution requires broad community input. As rising housing costs and weather extremes continue to put vulnerable populations at risk, Monday’s session aims to explore what resources, partnerships, and locations could make a dedicated day shelter on Capitol Hill a reality.
Residents interested in participating or learning more can attend the meeting or contact the organizers directly at daysheltercapitolhill@gmail.com .

articles.title: Single Shot owner sentenced to 13 months in prison in $1.5M payroll tax fraud case
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill restaurant Single Shot remains open as its owner has been sentenced to 13 months in prison and three years of supervised release for failing to pay more than $1.4 million in payroll taxes over a ten-year span, using some of the cash, federal prosecutors said in their announcement this week, to “remodel a home on Vashon Island.”

“This offense involves a significant breach of public trust,” U.S. District Judge Kimberly Evanson reportedly said during the sentencing hearing. “During the period when taxes were not being paid, he was spending on a home remodel, casino expenses, and travel.”

The announcement from the office of the United States Attorney for the Western District of Washington caps a legal process that first came to light this summer as prosecutors charged Rory McCormick with one count of Willful Failure to Pay Over Tax in the case that included $1,027,362 in unpaid employee taxes and another $418,979 in employer-side payroll taxes owed to the IRS .
McCormick agreed to plead guilty a week later .

According to the case documents, 87 employees at the restaurant had money withheld from their paychecks under the false premise that the taxes were being paid, reducing their actual take-home pay while their employer diverted the funds to personal luxuries. Because these payroll taxes were never sent to the IRS, several workers were left with uncredited gaps in their official work histories, jeopardizing their eligibility and lowering their future Social Security and Medicare retirement benefits, prosecutors say.

McCormick opened Single Shot on Summit in 2014, replacing a former photography gallery and helping grow a cluster of neighborhood food and drink on the block. CHS visited with Single Shot in December 2024 to mark its 10th anniversary neighboring The original Top Pot Doughnuts, Summit Public House, Cornelly, and Sol Liquor Lounge.

State filings show McCormick is the sole registered agent for Single Shot, the only restaurant named in the case. None of his other Seattle partnerships including Re:Public and El Grito Taqueria are involved in the charges.
Prosecutors said McCormick also admitted in his plea deal that he did not file his personal income taxes from any tax year 2015 through 2024.
The investigation found that McCormick spent nearly $400,000 buying and remodeling a home on Vashon Island, nearly $125,000 on casinos expenses, and more than $38,000 on travel over the decade.
He has been ordered to pay $1,446,341 in restitution as part of the deal.
A 13-month sentence is shorter than typical federal tax fraud cases of this scale. Standard sentencing guidelines usually recommend two to three years in prison for a theft of this size.
Because the term exceeds one year, McCormick qualifies for federal good-conduct credits which can reduce his actual time behind bars to roughly 11 months.
Single Shot has remained open at 611 Summit Ave E.

articles.title: Backing SFD overtime, funding for events like Umoja Fest, Madison Park traffic calming, and shutting down ‘spodies’ along Lake Washington — Hollingsworth’s ‘Day Two’ budget proposals
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Capitol Hill’s Fire Station 25 (Image: City of Seattle)

A second day of the Seattle City Council’s “Amendment Season” will continue the challenging balance of the city’s representatives pushing for constituent causes and district earmarks against a backdrop of reined-in spending as Mayor Katie Wilson tries to lead the way to a 2027-2028 budget that solves a potential $175 million deficit without cutting vital services or adding new taxes.

Wednesday’s council budget committee session will see representatives including District 3 leader Council President Joy Hollingsworth rolling out spending proposals across five departments: the Office of Economic Development, Seattle Department of Transportation, Seattle Fire Department, Office of Arts and Culture, and Seattle Parks and Recreation.

Justin Carder discusses the budget process and more on this week’s episode of the Seattle News, Views, and Brews podcast 2026 Episode 44: Budget Battles, RV Parking Bans, and More with Justin Carder, Capitol Hill Seattle Blog!

Hollingsworth’s “Day Two” firepower will mostly be put behind her co-sponsorships as aligns with colleagues in an attempt to restore front-line emergency capacity with $7.1 million for Seattle Fire Department overtime, funding ongoing pothole repair, supporting storefront vandalism recovery, and preserving a district-directed transportation project funding program that the mayor office wants scrapped and critics have complained is ineffective and inefficient.

Meanwhile, Hollingsworth’s lead amendments center heavily on cultural preservation in the Central District, localized quality-of-life improvements, and basic municipal services. As a prime sponsor, she is directing her focus toward the creative economy and economic equity by championing investments in underrepresented arts programming including $3 million for cultural initiatives in disadvantaged communities, backing for events like Umoja Fest and On The Block on Capitol Hill, and small business support via Tabor 100 , alongside targeted District 3 infrastructure improvements like Leschi and Madison Park pedestrian safety and Washington Park repairs.

CHS reported on Hollingsworth’s Day One priorities here the opening budget committee amendment session addressed 16 departments including the City Attorney’s office, civil rights, the Office of Housing , the Department of Neighborhoods , planning, finance, and utility spending.

With the focus on eliminating the deficit without cutting vital services, councilmembers are describing a limited playing field with little room for maneuvering or negotiation and are buttressing their district and neighborhood needs as part of wider citywide programs.

Tuesday, Hollingsworth soldiered on despite the deficit constrictions, advocating for and defending funding investments in her district such as $200,000 for the MLK F.A.M.E. Community Center and ongoing resources for the Central District and Southeast Seattle Reinvestment Fund , framing those proposals around historical equity, divestment, and community preservation.

“Standing up a sustainable fund that will continue to help direct funding to those communities with programming, cultural events, neighborhood events, building communities, and stimulating the economy is what we need in Seattle,” Hollingsworth said Tuesday about the $5 million reinvestment fund proposal.

Meanwhile, Wednesday, the D3 council member is also signing up for the city to take on the near impossible — shutting down high schoolers from organizing “spodies” — late night parties — in the city’s parks along Lake Washington.

Between Tuesday and Thursday, council members will review dozens of Council Budget Actions and Statements of Legislative Intent across City Hall before budget committee chair Dan Strauss unveils his balancing package next week.

articles.title: New Complaint Alleges Right-Wing Podcaster Brandi Kruse Is a Grassroots Lobbyist
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Skagit County freelance journalist and blogger Joe Kunzler agrees with many of right-wing podcaster Brandi Kruse’s views. In fact, he plans to vote for three initiative measures that Kruse strongly supports—revoking a new millionaires income tax, banning transgender girls from girls’ sports, and modifying some student privacy rights.

But Kunzler is disturbed by Kruse’s strong alliances with some conservative political interests while simultaneously claiming to be a member of the press. He’s filed a complaint with Washington’s Public Disclosure Commission (PDC), which regulates political finances in Washington, to request that it determine whether Kruse should be considered a grassroots lobbyist.

Many of Kunzler’s concerns have been raised by other parties—Kruse leading political rallies, her paid speeches at GOP functions, and her coziness with Let’s Go Washington, the political action committee responsible for the conservative statewide initiatives on November’s ballot. However, the potential lobbyist aspect is a previously unreported wrinkle.

According to the PDC, “direct lobbying” consists of dealing directly with legislators and government officials to influence state laws and policies. “Grassroots lobbying” consists of approaching the public to influence state laws and policies. People who lobby the Legislature for money, or possibly reimbursed travel, or have compiled lobby-related expenses must register with the PDC as a lobbyist.

The PDC’s disclosure requirements say : “Any person or entity making grassroots lobbying expenditures exceeding $1,500 in the aggregate in a one-month period or exceeding $3,000 in the aggregate in any three-month period must register as a sponsor of a grassroots lobbying campaign.”

Kunzler filed his complaint last March, and the PDC began its investigation in July. Kunzler’s complaint has been lost among higher-profile claims and counterclaims swirling about Kruse, who occupies a hazy spot in the Puget Sound media universe because she wears multiple press and political hats.
Kunzler’s complaint zeroes in on whether Kruse could be considered a lobbyist. “That should be part of the decision: Is she a lobbyist or not?” he said in an interview.
He alleges that Kruse—who is a leader of the movement to ban trans girls from girls’ sports—constantly switches roles to become whatever she needs to be.

“Brandi wants to be treated as a journalist when it benefits her. An activist when it benefits her. … Commercial media business, when she sells ads. A victim when somebody scrutinizes those ads. She wants all the benefits of influence and none of the accountability that comes with that influence. Sorry, that’s not how this works. If you build a platform around politics, you’re selling advertising, hosting events, appearing at rallies … you do not get to act shocked when someone asks whether disclosure laws apply to you,” he wrote in his complaint.
Illustrating Kunzler’s point, Kruse further clouded up the debate on if she is a journalist or activist last Friday at a Portland Thorns soccer match.

She helped lead a political stunt in which roughly 20 people wore XX/XY shirts—signifying opposition to transgender girls in girls’ sports—to the game, with the shirts deliberately hidden beneath coats. Then everyone took off their coats at halftime to display their XX/XY shirts.

OutKick columnist Matt Calkins had stationed himself nearby to cover the stunt. Calkins resigned from the Seattle Times in August over a spiked column about girl athletes wanting trans girls out of their sports.
The XX/XY reveal sparked an angry confrontation from trans-friendly Thorns fans, which was covered by Calkins
and Kruse. The arena’s security escorted Kruse and the rest of her group out to the street. Fox News reported Sunday that the US Department of Justice is investigating the incident.
“I wanna do my show. I’m not an activist,” Kruse said in a Saturday podcast about the confrontation.

The National Women’s Soccer League, including the Thorns, does not have an openly transgender player and doesn’t have a policy on trans players. Unlike in Washington, there is no anti-trans sports measure on Oregon’s ballot this November.
On Twitter Sunday , Kruse accused the crowd members that confronted her group of belonging to two Portland sports booster organizations that have ties to Antifa.
Meanwhile, Kruse declined to comment on Kunzler’s complaint to the PDC.

“I am not interested in participating in your breathless reporting about unfounded allegations against me. I’m sure The Stranger gets a lot of clicks when my name is in the headline,” she wrote in an email.
Last month, the PDC dismissed charges in an unrelated complaint that Kruse provided in-kind political donations to the three Let’s Go Washington ballot initiatives.

Months ago, Kruse and two right-wing allies filed a federal lawsuit against the Washington House clerk’s office and the Capitol Correspondents Association for denying the trio press passes to the Democratic side of the House chamber in Olympia because they are active in Republican political causes—sometimes for pay. Kruse despises the Olympia press corps, twice calling those reporters “enemies of the people” on her podcast.

The Capitol Correspondents Association recently dropped its opposition to granting them press passes, and the three dropped their suit against that group. Litigation is still in play against the House clerk’s office, with the judge voicing doubts that the plaintiffs will prevail.

Meanwhile, 570 KVI AM talk radio host Ari Hoffman, a Kruse ally and a plaintiff in the press pass litigation, has filed two PDC complaints against the Seattle Times , alleging that since private donations help fund its climate change and homelessness coverage, the newspaper is violating political finance laws, which should lead to denial of its Olympia press passes. Kruse has threatened similar complaints against other media entities, but has not followed through.

Kunzler noted Kruse has close relationships with Project 42 and its subsidiary Future 42, which is a daily advertiser on her podcast. Project 42’s leaders include Brian Heywood and Steve Gordon, who are also leaders of Let’s Go Washington, which has set up and financially backed seven public ballot measures for Washington voters since 2024. Their track record at the ballot box is three failed, one passed but later declared invalid, and three to be determined on Nov. 3.

Kruse is an “ambassador” for Future 42. Kunzler wants clarification on what that legally means. “Her ambassadorship raises lots of questions,” he said. The PDC is studying this same issue. Kunzler is suspicious about Kruse and Future 42 being in lockstep on most, if not all, political matters, and wants the PDC to examine that relationship.
In 2024 interviews , Kruse and Project 42 said they drifted together because of their similar political beliefs.
Kunzler also pointed to 2025 photographs of Kruse and Hoffman talking to GOP legislators in the House
Republican caucus room. Reporters and the public are not allowed in either party’s caucus meetings.

However, House GOP caucus chairman Peter Abbarno of Centralia said House Republicans routinely bring in people prior to caucus meetings to talk about their roles and what they do on their jobs—and this was one of those occasions. Other pre-caucus-meeting guest speakers include at least two mainstream media reporters plus Democratic Attorney General Nick Brown, he said.
“I do not want lobbyists with more access to state legislators,” Kunzler said.

articles.title: The Seattle Times Coverage of State Supreme Court Candidate Ian Birk is Partisan and Lopsided
articles.author: By John C. Alessio
paras: As someone who spent his life and career striving to help the disadvantaged, I was disappointed when Sean O’Donnell was endorsed by the Seattle Times over Ian Birk. From a progressive standpoint, Birk’s record is far superior to O’Donnell’s. The Seattle Times , perhaps concerned about Birk’s successes taking on corporations, concocted a runaway story challenging Birk’s ethical standing in the legal community. Their lopsided coverage of this race shows their own partisanship and their own concern for corporate interests.

On July 26, 2026, the Seattle Times endorsed Sean O’Donnell for State Supreme Court over Ian Birk. Typically, mainstream newspapers give relatively equal time to both candidates—favoring, of course, the candidate they want to endorse. This endorsement wasn’t like that. It was almost exclusively about O’Donnell, even though the editorial’s authors acknowledged both candidates were highly qualified. There was no recognition of the Washington State Court of Appeals on which Birk serves, being of a higher status than the King County Superior Court, on which O’Donnell sits. While they noted that Birk was elected unopposed, which is common when incumbent judges run for office, there was no mention of his extensive volunteer work through the King County Bar Association, including, for example, providing free legal assistance to disadvantaged people for over 10 years.

On September 14, 2026, the Times published an article on O’Donnell’s claim that Birk had violated judicial ethics by mentioning that O’Donnell was supported by the WA GOP. Birk’s claim about O’Donnell being a Republican is most likely true. O’Donnell received their endorsement. Anyone who has been involved in state politics knows that the WA GOP is highly unlikely to support anyone who is not a Republican or a Republican-agenda supporter. The state GOP endorsement is much different than endorsements by local Democratic legislative district organizations, which both O’Donnell and Birk list. Legislative districts are far less careful about who they endorse. Why doesn’t O’Donnell list the WA GOP as one of his endorsers as a sign of his bipartisan appeal? That endorsement isn’t on his website. He lists a number of Democratic organizations—why not the WA GOP? It seems that he is trying to hide his Republican affiliation.

On September 20, the Times again, this time as an editorial, attacked Birk , accusing him of taking his campaign into “the gutter”—retreading that same issue of Birk exposing O’Donnell’s political leanings.

And then on October 21 the Times , unbelievably, once again published yet another scathing attack on Ian Birk. Keying off that same tired issue, the Times posted innuendos of sleaziness—actually using terms like “sleazy hit jobs” without specifying what those activities were. As near as I can tell, the editorial’s authors are referring to the sources of Birk’s donations because they then state, “Roughly 80% of Birk’s total contributions come from personal injury firms, their attorneys and families.” They go on to say that only 1 percent of O’Donnell’s contributions come from such donors.

Well, it doesn’t take a genius to know that this difference is a function of the type of law the two attorneys practiced during their careers. O’Donnell was not a personal injury attorney; Birk was. The Times ’ editorial board heavily criticizes Birk and other personal injury attorneys for suing the state for millions of dollars. They neglect to include the millions such attorneys won for plaintiffs by suing megacorporations as well. Persons injured by corporate and government actions have the right to seek redress. Birk and other attorneys like him should be applauded for being good enough at their trade to take on the droves of corporate and state attorneys who defend the wrongdoers.

The vicious attacks on Ian Birk exemplify the Times ’ efforts to defend corporate interests, the interests of organizations like those endorsing Sean O’Donnell: Yakima Valley Landlords Association; Washington Retail Association ; Association of Washington Businesses ; the Central Washington Home Builders Association ; the Tacoma Business Council , etc.

The Times ’ relentless attack on Birk is unabashed partisan politics. The editorial board recognizes in Birk, who is endorsed by just about every well-known progressive organization in the state, a formidable opponent of their own conservative agenda. There is a reason the Times endorsed O’Donnell—not once, not twice, not thrice, but four times! They know where his heart is, just like the Republican Party knows.

Birk’s history involves making sure that all people have equal access to the protection of the law, and he has committed himself to maintaining that position. Washington voters should support Ian Birk. He is honest, fair, and brilliant. He will serve us well on the Washington State Supreme Court.

As for the issue of nonpartisan races, there is a great deal of misunderstanding about this concept. Races are identified as nonpartisan to prevent political parties from becoming involved. This does not mean the candidates running for nonpartisan races are nonpartisan. They still have ideological viewpoints. That includes judges. Just look at the United States Supreme Court. So, who do you prefer to run for office, someone who hides their political ideology or someone who makes no effort to do so? I prefer the latter, and that is the preference of just about everyone I talk to. People want to know who they are voting for. Ian Birk doesn’t come out and say what his political party preference is, which would be an ethics violation, but he makes no effort to hide who he is either. Those who try to hide who they are, like Sean O’Donnell, are being dishonest and doing the public a grave disservice.
John C. Alessio is a retired professor and university dean, and current Steilacoom resident . He is the author of multiple books.

articles.title: Slog AM: Owner of Single Shot Gets 13 Months in Prison, Man Climbs Fremont Construction Crane, Detroit Hairdresser Says Socialism Is Better Than What We Got Now
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: A federal judge sentenced Ruadhri “Rory” McCormick , the owner of Single Shot, a Capitol Hill restaurant, to 13 months in prison for not paying $1.4 million in payroll taxes. McCormick instead pocketed the money between 2014 and 2024. An investigation revealed he spent $400,000 on his Vashon Island home, flushed $125,000 into casinos, and dropped $38,000 for trips. McCormick also didn’t pay his personal income taxes between 2015 and 2024.

October clouds, we need a timeout. What in the world is eating you? Despite being thick and dark and low in the sky, you’re not letting go of your water. We very well know it’s in you. We can see it with our very own eyes. But, you keep on keeping it to yourselves as you pass over the city. What gives? Sure, there were some showers this weekend, but Monday, like Tuesday, saw almost none at all. Where do you clouds think you’re going with all your water? I’m asking this for the Columbia City trees and other puzzled plants. Expect a high 53 today. Also expect no rain on Halloween.

More on Microsoft’s voluntary exits for around a quarter of its workforce . The offer, which the tech giant made to employees in Canada, India, the UK, and the US, expires in early December. If accepted, you have to bounce on the last day of the year. Predictably, many are blaming AI for this dismal state of affairs. Robots are replacing humans because they are “ better, stronger, faster ” and, most important of all, cheaper. But a close examination of the matter is not required to plainly see what’s really going on: AI isn’t making nearly as much money as the massive amounts of borrowed cash being pumped into it on the regular. The logical thing to do, under these circumstances, would be to pull the plug on the unprofitable machine; but, instead, Microsoft and other tech corporations are pulling the plug on workers for short-term gains.
By the way, Microsoft’s total revenue in 2025 was nearly $300 billion . And its bottom line (or net income, or net profit) was just above $100 billion.

Old, and even worthless, is the idea that finance represents a late-stage expression of capitalism. The conclusion of this way of thinking is that the more the honorable business of making money from making things produces profits that don’t make the eyes of executives water or pop, then the more they turn to the funny phantom money of capital markets. But I think a more accurate reading of finance places its moment of flight not at the dusk of productive capitalism, like Hegel’s owl of minerva . Its moment arrives, instead, with the rise and shine of the sun. You don’t have capitalism without the swirl of speculative bubbles.

When asked by the BBC if Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is too radica l, too far to the left,⁠ Nicole Williams, a Detroit hairdresser, said it like it is : “Socialist, socialize, social, don’t matter to me, lower my cost of living!”

One of the key characteristics of capitalism is that it collapses or goes into crisis when its growth is zero or negative. It cannot survive without the positive feedback of money making more money, which is why it needs, for its movement, a propeller with these blades: the production of luxuries like penthouses, and the production of a prodigious amount of waste (and this is why recycling is, in essence, anti-capitalist). Put another way, capitalism does not, one, make life cheaper, but more expensive (which explains its rabid resistance to public forms of transportation, housing, and health insurance—they are more efficient, and therefore not costly); and, two, it must maintain an energy flow that moves not in cycles, but is uni-directional: from extraction to production to, whenever possible, permanent destruction (disposability).

At around 12:35 a.m. on Tuesday , a young man was spotted climbing a crane that rose high above Fremont. What was he up to ? Maybe trying to reach the moon, which was pretty full that night (October’s Hunter’s Moon appeared the day before)? The climber managed to reach “20 to 30 stories high” before the police arrived, brought him “ straight back down, down to earth ,” and arrested him for “reckless endangerment.”

Fremont’s crane/moon incident not only recalled, for me, a line from a hit tune by a forgotten Brit pop band, Curiosity Killed the Cat, that made old Andy Warhol way too thirsty, it also recalled this passage from W.G. Sebald’s novel Austerlitz : “We are not alone in dreaming at night for, quite apart from dogs and other domestic creatures whose emotions have been bound up with ours for many thousands of years, the smaller mammals such as mice and moles also live in a world that exists only in their minds whilst they are asleep, as we can detect from their eye movements, and who knows, said Austerlitz, perhaps moths dream as well, perhaps a lettuce in the garden dreams as it looks up at the moon by night.”

Like father, like son. Or the apple does not fall far from the tree. Or cut from the same cloth. Or some other similar saying. So, after losing Brazil’s presidential election, far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president of Brazil Jair Bolsonaro (he is doing to time for attempting to pull a Jan 6 after losing the election in 2023), got onto a jet with his family and fled the country . He has now landed in Florida to lick his wounds before the president of the United States of America. The winner of the election, socialist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, described the whole sorry business as “shameful.” Bolsonaro is not a straight shooter. Dark money swirls around him like the autumn leaves swirled around me yesterday, as I walked at dusk from Hillman City to Columbia City. Bolsonaro is expected to request political asylum.

Let’s end AM with Ice Cube’s “Alive on Arrival,” which will be one of the tracks I discuss with Dr. Daudi Abe and Vitamin D during tomorrow’s See You at the Crossroads: Death In Hip Hop show at Black & Tan Hall. Abe’s description of the track: “This story of the dangers and pitfalls of urban life is also a scathing critique of police mistreatment and indifference and a dysfunctional health care system. After being shot, the storyteller winds up lying on the floor of an emergency room and then handcuffed to a bed. The on-beat beep of a heart monitor punctuates the climax of the song, which concludes suddenly with a flatline.”

articles.title: ‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory
articles.author: Ryan Gilbey
paras: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up

When Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their native Spain as “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movie ever .’” Job done.

At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip film Fatherland . La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together.
