articles.title: 3 major issues that Republican Byron Donalds or Democrat David Jolly will need to address as Florida’s next governor
articles.author:
<name>Liv Coleman, Professor of Political Science and International Studies, University of Tampa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/liv-coleman-2758243"/>
paras: After nearly three decades of Republican control of Florida, the executive office of the governor has become more powerful than ever before.
So when Florida voters choose between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly for governor on Nov. 3, the winner will be poised to shape the state’s direction for years to come.

I’m a political scientist who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. I’ve been watching how the two candidates say they will use their authority to shape policy around healthcare, education and home rule – and what help they might need from the Legislature.

One of the first choices awaiting the new governor will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position created in 2007 . The surgeon general oversees the Florida Department of Health and county health departments across the state.

The position comes with the power to declare public health emergencies , forcibly quarantine people and set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of seven childhood vaccine mandates .

As part of his conservative remake of Florida policies , Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, Dr. Joseph Ladapo , to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading medical freedom advocate and vaccine skeptic.

Ladapo opposes all vaccine mandates . At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he recommended against COVID-19 vaccinations for healthy children and ended quarantine mandates for Florida public schoolchildren exposed to COVID-19. He also said that he wanted mRNA vaccines “not to be available to anyone” in the state.

Ladapo also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to drop mandates for four vaccines required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows exemptions only for approved religious or medical reasons.
The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes the rule change on public health grounds.

Donalds has long opposed vaccine mandates and says that he did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine . He supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change to reduce school vaccination mandates and says he is open to reappointing Ladapo as surgeon general.

Jolly, on the other hand, supports Florida’s current school vaccine mandates and exemptions . He says he would fire Ladapo on Day 1 in favor of someone who “ embraces science and evidence-based public health .”

No matter which candidate is elected governor, the Florida Legislature has tied his hands on how far he can push vaccine policy. The Legislature has mandated measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law. It also stripped the surgeon general of the power to enforce vaccine mandates during public health emergencies in November 2021, during the pandemic.

One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of universal vouchers by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows parents of any income level to use US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence , for their children’s private or homeschooling education.

The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026 . State auditors have identified accountability problems in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced declining enrollment , with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.

Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program, recounting how his family saved money for him to attend a private high school . Donalds has touted universal vouchers in Christian nationalist circles and expressed an interest in making Florida “ the model state for school choice ” by allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace .
His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a network of for-profit charter schools and advocates nationally for school choice .

The only change Donalds has proposed is a universal scorecard for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.

Jolly also supports the universal voucher program but wants significant changes. Jolly personally sends his own two children to private, faith-based schools with the support of vouchers . He says private schools that accept vouchers should meet the same standards and requirements as public schools , including the mandate to serve students with disabilities. He also wants to limit private school tuition to the value of the voucher and reinstate benefit eligibility based on financial need .
Campaign promises aside, neither candidate can do much to affect the universal voucher program, because it was created by the Legislature.

Democrat Jolly knows he would need the Legislature’s cooperation to advance reforms and claims that he has identified Republican allies to do so. Donalds would likely face a friendly Republican majority for his more modest proposed reforms.

The next Florida governor will also be able to influence state education policy by appointing the seven members of the Board of Education and then recommending a candidate for commissioner of education for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the Florida Department of Education and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.
The position of commissioner used to be elected, but in 2002 voters approved a constitutional amendment creating the current system, which gives more power to the governor.

The next governor’s appointees to the Board of Education could try to shape the effects of universal vouchers more indirectly. The board could approve an annual legislative budget request with new recommended funding levels for public education to make up for shortfalls due to revenue loss from vouchers.
They could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, as the DeSantis administration has done .
In general, Jolly says he intends to use executive authority as vigorously as possible in education, as DeSantis did, particularly to promote diversity programs.
A third hot-button topic facing the next governor is home rule , or the principle that local governments, such as cities and counties, should be able to set policy on local issues.

The DeSantis administration severely eroded home rule. The governor signed legislation limiting local controls over land development . This bill restricted the ability of Manatee County, for example, to protect wetlands under the guise of emergency management legislation.

He also required counties to cooperate with federal immigration authorities and put counties under DOGE-style audits . He even removed local elected officials from office . For example, he ousted a pair of popular Democratic state attorneys , Hillsborough County State Attorney Andrew Warren and State Attorney Monique Worrell of Orange and Osceola counties, alleging neglect of duty in both cases. By August 2023, DeSantis had removed 23 elected officials, a number much larger than his predecessors .

Donalds has affirmed that he supports the steps DeSantis has taken and plans to take executive authority further , scheduling more DOGE audits of local government and removing more elected officials as needed.

In contrast, Jolly says he would counter DeSantis on home rule. He wants local authorities to decide budgets and policy on their own. He sees removing elected officials as an affront to the democratic process .

What to do about large-scale data centers, however, scrambles home rule for the candidates. Donalds wants local communities to be able to decide whether to build data centers. But Jolly, citing concerns about the health and environmental effects of data centers, wants a statewide moratorium on new data center construction for one year and is open to a permanent ban .

Voters will have an important say of their own on home rule when they vote on Amendment 3 , which would substantially lower homestead property taxes. Critics warn that if it passes, local governments will likely have to turn to Tallahassee to make up for lost funds, and strings will be attached.
Donalds supports Amendment 3, while Jolly opposes it.
Liv Coleman is affiliated with the Manatee County Democratic Party.

articles.title: 1 in 4 Pennsylvanians say they paid out of pocket for their annual checkup. Why isn’t insurance covering these preventive visits?
articles.author:
<name>Sujeong Park, Assistant Professor of Health Policy and Addiction Studies, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sujeong-park-2768782"/>
paras: I was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act , or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing.

The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care.
Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too.

The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA.

When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero.

As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time?

Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup.

Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles . A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying.

The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services , including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients.
Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free.

If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible.
Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred.

Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits . But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket.

Our study , published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll , an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year.
Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50.

After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100.
Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable.

Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate.

I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings . Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective.

Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care.

Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge.

If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision.
A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed.

Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs.

articles.title: Some states are stepping up after federal childcare cuts – and now offer lessons for the future
articles.author:
<name>Caitlyn Collins, Associate Professor of Sociology, Washington University in St. Louis</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/caitlyn-collins-1136368"/>
paras: While affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs , one important expense often gets less attention – childcare.

After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “ childcare cliff ,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket.

The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare.

But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system .

Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families.

As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work.

Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets.

The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape.

Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care.
The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children . Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid.

As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country.

One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support , the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees.

Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers , the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program.

New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare . Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income.
Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year.

Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children.

The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties.

Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots , although the rollout in September hit bumps .

Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey . That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier.

On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy.

Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working.

The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility . And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent.

Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays.

These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG.

The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway.
We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components.

First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market.

Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care.

Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs.

Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest.

articles.title: Falcon 9 ushered in the modern space economy – retiring it could leave the industry vulnerable
articles.author:
<name>Mojtaba Akhavan-Tafti, Research Associate Professor, Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mojtaba-akhavan-tafti-2299913"/>
paras: More than 50% of the nearly 330 spaceflights to low Earth orbit in 2025 were done on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Falcon 9 is much smaller than SpaceX’s flashy Starship rocket, but for the past 16 years it has been a reliable choice for launching satellites to orbit.

It has carried payloads ranging from Earth-imaging sensors feeding smartphone map apps to environmental monitoring satellites that track wildfires. It has also launched the crew capsule that ferries astronauts to the International Space Station.
In late 2026, reports came out that SpaceX is shuffling its staff in an attempt to focus its resources on developing and commercializing Starship, while phasing out the Falcon 9.

At face value, this sounds like routine news; after all, companies shuffle resources all the time. But as a space scientist , I believe that retiring this rocket threatens to suffocate the commercial space industry that it helped bring to life – unless the public and private sectors step up their efforts to fill the gap Falcon 9’s retirement has created.

Since its inception in 2002, SpaceX has broadened access to space. In 2006, while facing the looming retirement of the space shuttle , NASA searched for a private alternative to resupply the International Space Station. The agency awarded companies contracts, and SpaceX’s award helped kick-start the development of Falcon 9.

Despite multiple near-bankruptcy setbacks, Falcon 9 made its inaugural test flight in 2010, followed by sending the SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule to its first docking at the International Space Station in 2012.

The real turning point came in 2015 with the first successful landing of a Falcon 9 booster . The booster is the rocket’s main first stage. It houses fuel tanks and nine main engines. It provides the primary thrust off the launchpad but detaches from the rest of the rocket shortly after. Landing the booster meant SpaceX could recover and refly this component and dramatically slash launch costs .

In the meantime, Boeing, the other NASA contract awardee, struggled with budget overruns and operational delays . Some of SpaceX’s other competitors, such as Blue Origin, pivoted toward suborbital space tourism . As a result, Falcon 9 did more than just capture the market. It effectively became the market.

SpaceX’s affordable and frequent access to space helped to breathe life into a booming space economy. It allowed startups with creative new business models to send their satellites to orbit, such as TakeMe2Space , an Indian startup exploring hosting data centers in orbit. It empowered governments around the world to dramatically expand their operations in space, including governments relying on SpaceX’s secured communication platform, named Starshield .

Then came the operational shift. In July 2026, accounts from prospective commercial customers and satellite operators revealed that SpaceX had begun turning away Falcon 9 customers to focus its resources on the more capable Starship rocket.

Almost overnight, the announcement threatened to freeze the pipeline of launches the market relied on. Those who can afford it are paying extra to secure the few remaining slots on Falcon 9, while others are scrambling to find alternative launch opportunities. While European customers are generally flocking to the European Space Agency’s Ariane 6 rocket, others are booking slots on upcoming medium-lift rockets, such as Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket .

SpaceX is contractually obligated to continue Falcon 9 flights for NASA’s International Space Station crew rotations and other national security payloads. However, the rest of the space industry is now forced to buy into SpaceX’s Starship bet . There simply is no operational alternative today that can match Falcon 9’s combination of high launch cadence, affordable pricing and proven flight heritage for medium-class payloads.

When a single company is put in charge of controlling the gate to space, its internal corporate decisions can make or break an industry. That also makes the company a potential single point of failure , where a setback by a single vendor would paralyze the entire space economy.

The U.S. has dealt with this type of national security dilemma before. In the 1900s, Standard Oil owned critical oil production infrastructure , pipelines and railroads. Controlling critical pipeline networks gave the company unprecedented power to set transport terms, prioritize its own shipments and restrict pipeline access for independent oil producers. This structure meant competitors had no viable alternative transport routes. Ultimately, this forced the U.S. government to intervene because internal Standard Oil corporate decisions dictated market dynamics.

Standard Oil had become the gatekeeper to the free flow of oil. By addressing that potential single point of failure, the U.S. government nudged an industry to redefine itself, which led to its accelerated growth.
SpaceX took huge technical and financial bets on the success of Falcon 9. They paid off and led to SpaceX’s market dominance .

But now SpaceX wants to do it again, with the promise that Starship would help further reduce the cost of getting to space. Their vision is grand, but what happens if Starship experiences delays ? What happens to companies who relied on Falcon 9?

As SpaceX shifts focus, competing launch providers will likely rush to take advantage of this market opportunity and offer rides to customers being turned away by SpaceX, but at a steep premium. The customers also face the burden of reconfiguring their satellites to fit on another rocket.

This sudden market shift has been a wake-up call , one that I believe will cost the industry and add significant uncertainty to market dynamics in a few years. But it also offers the market an opportunity to correct course by filling the gap that Falcon 9’s retirement has created.

Over the past two decades, NASA has successfully delivered on its mandate to create a rocket-launch marketplace. To achieve this, NASA fundamentally shifted from operating government-owned hardware to buying fixed-price services. This meant that NASA became a reliable anchor customer whose contracts spurred competition among commercial providers.
While this model proved that routine, low-cost space access was achievable, various technical and business challenges allowed the marketplace to become dominated by a single vendor.

Moving forward, NASA and other public agencies can work together to strategically distribute the payloads they need to launch across commercial rockets built by other companies. These government contracts can help these companies improve and validate their emerging rocket programs . Satellite customers can design standardized payloads that work across multiple types of rockets, so they don’t rely on one launch provider.

NASA can also maintain its dedicated launch assistance programs . Subsidizing these slots would allow smaller institutions, such as academia and nonprofit organizations, to avoid competing on the open market against large companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin that launch satellites regularly. These programs help smaller institutions that may not have the funds to directly buy their own spot on a rocket get their payload to space. These payloads are often used to give students experience and help train the next generation of space workers exploring the cosmos.

Mojtaba Akhavan-Tafti does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: ‘Let nothing be forgotten’: Holocaust survivors’ memorial books honored lives lost and vibrant hometowns
articles.author:
<name>Jennifer Rich, Professor of Sociology, Rowan University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jennifer-rich-485730"/>
paras: My grandmother was a Holocaust survivor from Kostopol, Ukraine. Years after she passed away, I was trying to learn more about her life before the war – something I knew very little about. When I found a book called “Sefer Kostopol” – Hebrew for “Book of Kostopol” – I hoped to find her among its pages.

It was a memorial book for her hometown, but beyond that, I wasn’t sure what to make of it. I’m a scholar of Holocaust memory , but I had never come across anything quite like it. It was a bit like a scrapbook, with varied types of images, essays written by different residents and lists of survivors – where I found my grandmother’s name – and of their murdered families, including her mother and sister.
My questions led me to investigate exactly what “Sefer Kostopol” was – and to learn that communities of survivors created over 1,000 such memorial books, called “yizker bikher” in Yiddish .

After the Holocaust, Eastern European survivors and Jews who had left before the war created these memorial books to honor their destroyed towns and murdered loved ones. Devoted to their neighbors, these collaboratively written volumes were one way for survivors to reclaim their lives and memories.

Yizker bikher were created not only to document the destruction of the Nazi genocide, but also to preserve the everyday lives that came before it. The volumes insist that Jewish communities be remembered not solely as sites of death but as places where people lived, argued, worked and celebrated. In general, around two-thirds of a given volume is devoted to describing prewar life; the remaining third includes first-person accounts of the Nazi occupation of the town and a long list of the dead.

Each book had anywhere from 20 to 50, even 75, contributors, who wrote in a warm, colloquial style. The visuals, too, feel personal. Photos portray the particulars of prewar life, with images of sports teams, school groups, bustling market squares and busy, modern streets.

Another common feature are maps, almost always drawn and labeled from memory by a survivor: the details of the forests and the rivers, the nicknames that locals used for the streets and stories of the homes and shops.

Beyond the photographs and maps, most volumes contain sketches by amateur artists to convey information about life under Nazi occupation. Some include art by well-known artists at the time, like Arthur Szyk , a Polish-Jewish illustrator and political cartoonist. There are also ephemera like posters, budgets, song lyrics, book covers, event flyers and elementary school report cards.

The earliest volume that I studied came from Volkovisk, Belarus, and was published in 1946, just a year after the liberation of Auschwitz . It’s hard to imagine survivors finding one another and putting books together so soon after the war.

The editors, publication committees and contributors, though, reached for a familiar model: the “pinkes,” the community register found in every Eastern European Jewish town. These books contained everything from meeting minutes to school budgets and lists of political candidates.
Like the community registers, yizker bikher have a somewhat chaotic, idiosyncratic organization to them. Both were written by many hands, and they became treasured objects.

The relationship was so strong that many yizker bikher include the word “pinkes” in their title. In the introductions, some editors made explicit connections between the prewar pinkes and those created in the wake of the Holocaust. One of them was Eliezer Yerushalmi, who compiled the memorial book from Navaredok, Belarus .

Each pinkes is a link in a timeless chain recording the history of Jewish communities, he wrote: “The present pinkes, the Navaredok pinkes, is here to tell the orphaned generation and the generations to come all that the community experienced from its very beginning hundreds of years ago to its terrible destruction.”

Just like Jewish communities in Eastern Europe were interconnected, so too were survivor communities in places like the United States, Canada, Israel and Argentina. Some yizker bikher committees relied on the same editors and adopted features of other memorial books , making the process easier.

The first step was for members of the book committee to circulate a prospectus to their fellow survivors to explain the memorial project. A prospectus for the “Wielun Memorial Book,” commemorating a community in Poland, was circulated in 1961, 10 years before the volume was published. The editor wrote that,
That goal – “let nothing be forgotten” – sits at the very heart of each memorial book.

Despite this, yizker bikher were mostly overlooked by scholars for many years. Perhaps this was because they defy easy categories: They are too nostalgic to be histories and too historical to be literature. They are too secular to be religious and too religious to be secular. And the range of visual material complicates things even further – for example, they aren’t photo albums per se, but they certainly include hundreds of photographs.

In the past few years, however, there has been a surge of academic and popular interest . Scholars are exploring the books and the archives that created them to learn more about all aspects of prewar Jewish life. They have also used yizker bikher to understand the intimate nature of the violence wrought by the Nazis and their local collaborators, and the beautiful, profound ways survivors found to honor their loved ones.

When we take yizker bikher seriously, it allows us to expand our focus beyond how 6 million Jews were murdered and highlight the way they once lived. Ultimately, these books remember individuals and communities as they wanted to be remembered.

articles.title: Plans with cheaper premiums are risky business for Americans seeking lower healthcare costs
articles.author:
<name>Thomas Buchmueller, Professor of Business Economics and Public Policy, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/thomas-buchmueller-2768566"/>
paras: Healthcare costs are a major concern for Americans , and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety .

Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options.

We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers .
But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive.
People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks.

Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014 , insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether.

The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination , established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces .
Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape.

Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums , the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers.
Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious.

As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons.

First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses.

Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans.
Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers , short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states .

Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries , arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance.

Because they are not regulated as insurance companies , healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim.

Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits.

Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau . These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture.

These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers . Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage.
Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option.

If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy . And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections.
If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself:

Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage . This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance.

If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive.

Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance.

Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be.

Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. In 2011-2012 he was the Senior Health Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and from 2023-2025 he was Deputy Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Helen Levy was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. She served as a Senior Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers in 2010-2011.

articles.title: How the Federal Way Link Extension Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: In December 2025, Sound Transit welcomed the first passengers aboard the Federal Way Link Extension. The three new stations on the 1 Line provide improved transit connectivity for many south King County residents. An accompanying bus service change in March 2026 improved frequency on many bus routes and adjusted a few bus routes to better connect with the new Link stations. While some routes lost ridership, many other routes welcomed new passengers. Link increased the total number of transit trips in south King County with nearly 10,000 combined weekday boardings at Federal Way, Star Lake, and Kent Des Moines stations.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in south King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.

Route 181 serves as the primary east-west route between Federal Way and Auburn. Federal Way Transit Center has long been a busy stop as it connects passengers with many other bus routes. The new Federal Way Link station caused a 46% increase in Route 181 boardings at that stop each day, from 293 to 430 passengers. Overall ridership on Route 181 increased by about 114 passengers and the ridership at other stops was not significantly impacted.

Route 183 is a coverage route between Federal Way and Kent, via the new Star Lake station. Prior to the Federal Way Link Extension, the route connected to freeway bus routes 177, 193, and 574 at I-5 & 272nd St. That connection generated about 4 boardings per day for Route 183. Now, 71 passengers board Route 183 each weekday at Star Lake station, a 1,675% increase. This is still just a fraction of the 1,600 weekday Link boardings at the station as many Link passengers use the station’s 1,100 space parking garage. Both of the route’s termini, Federal Way and Kent, have a slight decrease in ridership. This may be from some passengers switching to Link at Star Lake rather than to another bus in Federal Way or Kent.

The A Line now runs in the 1 Line’s shadow between Federal Way and Tukwila. Thanks to fast and frequent service along Pacific Hwy, it was the most productive Metro route in 2024 . Now that Link offers a faster trip north from Federal Way, this title may be in trouble. Stops across the A Line have reduced ridership from 2025. At Federal Way Transit Center, boardings on the A Line have dropped 19%. Likewise, the number of passengers boarding the A Line at Pacific Hwy & 240th St (near Kent Des Moines station) has been cut in half. Part of this severe drop in boardings is due to the new A Line stop that opened next to Kent Des Moines station. When factoring in boardings at that stop, there is still a 24% decrease in A Line boardings near Kent Des Moines station. A similar change occurred at International Blvd & 200th St, next to Angle Lake station. Many passengers who previously rode the A Line to the Link 1 Line’s southern terminus in 2025 are now opting to board Link at one of the new stations. Despite this drop in ridership, the A Line still provides critical local service along Pacific Hwy. As the area continues to develop, ridership on the A Line will rebound.

Route 165 connected Burien and Des Moines with Kent and Auburn via the newly opened Kent Des Moines Link station. Since the new station opened, boardings on Route 165 at the nearby stops (Pacific Hwy & KDM Rd, KDM Station, Pacific Hwy & 240th St) have increased 50% (109 daily passengers). This increase is offset by 70 fewer boardings at Kent Sounder Station, suggesting some passengers have switched from Sounder to Link. The route’s termini both have slightly reduced boarding counts as well, likely also due to the new station. For instance, someone traveling between Normandy Park and downtown Seattle may have switched from the 165 + H Line to 165 + 1 Line for their trip. In August 2026, Route 165 was replaced by routes 164 and 166.

The Federal Way Link Extension also impacted a few Sound Transit Express bus routes. As these routes are operated by Pierce Transit, we do not have detailed ridership data for them (yet). Instead, this analysis will use the overall route ridership comparing April 2025 to April 2026.

Ridership on Route 574 increased about 10% year-over-year. This is mostly from more people traveling between Lakewood or Tacoma and Link in Federal Way. Route 574 previously connected with Link at SeaTac, so the FWLE likely did not attract too many new passengers. The August 2026 service change truncated Route 574 at Federal Way in exchange for a much needed frequency boost, which should further increase ridership.

Routes 577 and 578 form the primary bus connection between downtown Seattle and Federal Way. Most times of the day, these routes are still faster than Link for that trip. As a result, ridership has not changed too dramatically. Boardings are down 10% on both routes. Routes 577 and 578 both saw a more significant drop in ridership immediately after the FWLE opening in December, but ridership has since rebounded. Whether the recent ridership increases are due to the routes’ lower travel time or due to the World Cup and other seasonal ridership changes is still up in the air.

The Federal Way Link Extension is already making its mark on travel patterns in south King County. Local routes connecting with Link are busier than last year. Meanwhile, ST Express routes and the RapidRide A Line lost some passengers to Link. The August 2026 service change further improved local connectivity in south King County that should make transit the best option for even more trips.

While this article only covered a few routes, detailed ridership data for most King County Metro routes is now updated at seattletransitridership.com . In addition, the impact of the Crosslake Connection on bus routes in east King County was discussed in a recent article .

articles.title: Op-Ed: The Case for Public Access at University Swimming Pools
articles.author: Collin Reid
paras: What is the community function of a university? Beyond employment, labs, and lecture halls, one underappreciated tertiary benefit is maintaining a walkable urban ecosystem as a model for urban design. For many Americans raised in the sprawling suburbs, university is the first and last time they live in a walkable community. Although universities possess neither the political nor material resources to reshape the entire national urban ecosystem, they can – and sometimes do – enhance their local communities by opening their recreational facilities to the public.

Pools are just one example of where universities could make a significant material contribution to their urban ecosystems. While opening both pools and fitness centers would be ideal, as universities could use the revenue generated to supplement student fees and theoretically decrease the cost of education, the community impact of a new pool would be far more significant.

This is because commercial fitness centers are significantly less capital intensive than pools, costing a few hundred thousand dollars to open, with the most basic facilities costing below $100,000 and only the largest most advanced facilities breaking into the millions. On the other hand, indoor commercial pools typically run into the tens of millions , and that’s before land acquisition.

The city of Shoreline is currently providing a pertinent insight into the financial cost and community value of a centrally located public pool. The city has placed Proposition 1 on this November’s ballot, where residents will vote on the construction of an aquatics facility to replace the one it closed in 2020 with an estimated cost of $100 million factoring in projected inflation by 2028 and 15% design contingencies. The design includes a leisure pool with a lazy river, a hot tub alongside a sauna, and an eight-lane 25-yard lap pool with diving boards.

Located in the heart of Shoreline at Midvale and 178th Street, the proposed pool will be within walking distance of the E, Route 333, and 348 bus lines, Shorewood High School, and multiple supermarkets. Successful passage would triple the year-round pool space open to the public in Shoreline, as the Dale Turner YMCA has a four-lane lap pool and a smaller leisure pool, and allow residents the opportunity to swim for a lower price while supporting their local government.

Pools are so expensive because the engineering behind them is complex: you don’t need precision angling of cement to plop some mats, barbells, and workout machines in a basic gym. The solution to increasing their availability isn’t to ignore regulations, but to recognize that the cheapest infrastructure is that which already exists. Evergreen Aquatics Center recognized this, opting to save a facility from demolition back in 2009, which saved the public tens of millions in financial and community value.

For the purposes of quantification, I’ll evaluate the ability of pools to serve lap swimming while acknowledging that pools can serve a wide variety of functions of varying capacities. All the publicly accessible indoor pools in Seattle have 79 lap lanes in total. Each lane can host eight swimmers (though I personally think sharing a lane with more than four people feels crowded), so all the publicly available pools in Seattle can host 632 lap swimmers at once at maximum capacity (316 comfortably).

All the public pools in Seattle have six lanes, and they offer the majority of space in this calculation. However, it is exceedingly rare that all lanes are open at public pools, especially in the afternoon when they have to balance demand with swimming lessons and other activities. This generally results in about one to two hours of lap swim available in the afternoon. By opening University of Washington’s 14-lane IMA pool and University of Seattle’s two six-lane pools for even just two hours of public lap swimming, these institutions would effectively add more than four public pools’ worth of lanes, absorbing demand to relieve crowding at public pools and potentially opening time and space to expand the variety of activities available.

In explaining why University of Washington’s pool isn’t open to the public, Assistant Director of Operations for Recreation, Chad Yarbrough, pointed to deference to tuition-paying students who fund the facility: “The IMA (Student Recreation Center) is not open to the general public because of space limitations and because access to the facility is funded through fees paid by UW students as part of their tuition.”
When asked whether the university had considered opening to the public before, he confirmed they had: “Yes. We have discussed these options before, however, [we] are not going in that direction.”

Seattle University was more amenable to the idea of public access, as they already partner with local swim teams who rent their facility on a regular basis. Assistant Director of UREC, Melissa Wessel, explained that the pools are currently closed to the wider public because “we don't have an easy way for folks who aren't a part of a specific group or UREC members to currently swim as building-wide access could be an issue. We are currently exploring more ways to better serve the Seattle swim community.”

Along with relieving demand for public pools, UW and Seattle U could also enhance the walkability and bikeability of the urban ecosystem. Seattle U’s central location in a relatively dense urban area could pedestrianize a number of trips, and University of Washington’s pool is about a quarter mile from the Link station bearing the public institution’s name. From a transit perspective, University of Washington’s pool would further capitalize upon the apparent decision to prioritize traffic flows to stadiums when designing the Link and planning bus lines.

Because Seattle already hosts a decent amount of public and private pools accessible via transit throughout the city, opening university pools to the public would most likely relieve demand for lap swimming at public pools while integrating more people into the community spirits they already engender among alumni and with other programs. This is particularly true for Seattle U, where there are two YMCA pools and the public Medgar Evers pool all located close by and easily accessed via transit. It’s outside of Seattle, in cities like Tacoma and Bellingham, where universities like Puget Sound, Pacific Lutheran, and Western Washington have the potential to make the greatest impact on their local communities.

Like Seattle U, University of Puget Sound (UPS) has options for people to swim somewhat nearby and is somewhat accessible via transit. However, as central Tacoma has only two bus routes of 30-60 minute frequency that both primarily feed into downtown (the 11 and the 16), this leaves the area significantly car dependent. However, the Pierce County bus expansions contained within Proposition 1 on the ballot this November offer the opportunity to greatly boost service, if it passes.

UPS’s eight-lane pool would significantly contribute to the walkability and usefulness of transit to its surrounding area if it opened to the public. With more frequent transit and a proper north-south route along Union Avenue or Alder Street, the greenspace and facilities of UPS would have even more potential to serve as a walkable and transit-oriented community hub, decreasing car dependency and generating a more localized sense of place. Unfortunately, UPS didn’t respond to my inquiries, and there is no evidence that they have any plans to capitalize upon their potential in this regard.

Further south, technically south of Tacoma, lies the Census Designated Place of Parkland, a former streetcar suburb with Pacific Lutheran University (PLU) right at its heart and along the (in)famous Route 1 down Pacific Avenue, Pierce County’s most used bus route, which ironically had once had rails. Pacific Avenue has become a prototypical sprawl-based stroad in the decades since the rails were torn away all while the area has been suffering from poverty, violence, and neglect from the government. The poverty and violence have created a stigma about the area that can cause people to write it off, and a somewhat recent example of this neglect arose with the now abandoned bus rapid transit (BRT) system to serve Pacific Avenue.

The people of Parkland do not deserve this stigma and neglect, and PLU’s location at the community’s heart places it in a perfect position to pump vibrancy back into the area if it allows the people to circulate through its system.

To its credit, PLU has taken steps to offer services to the community and begin the process of serving as a hub: the public can and does utilize its beautiful greenspaces, it plans to open a medical clinic in partnership with MultiCare , and they offer free tutoring and English Language Learning (ELL) classes at the Parkland Literacy Center. These are all good starts, especially if the clinic offers free or at least discounted services to members of the community regardless of whether they meet the strict requirements for Medicare.
When it comes to PLU’s pool, the institution has taken some very small steps by hosting affordable public swim lessons, but remains committed to keeping the pool closed to the public beyond that.

“Because the pool’s operations are funded directly by student tuition, our schedule must prioritize the intensive demands of our varsity athletic programs, student intramurals, and campus recreation," PLU’s director of digital communications Christopher Albert said. "We do not offer general public open-swim hours to ensure our students have full access to the resources essential to their collegiate experience, while keeping our public engagement focused on high-value safety programs.”

Though swimming lessons are useful, is there not a certain irony to teaching people how to swim and then not offering any window of time, however brief, to use the only lap pool in their community? The pool’s location within walking distance of Keithley Middle School, Washington High School, and blocks upon blocks of residential housing has the potential to serve as a meaningful third space, even if open to the public for only a couple hours a week, and would synergize with the steps the university is taking towards community integration. If the issue is funding, even a small membership fee would go a long way with sustained public participation.

Examining the greater Tacoma region as a whole, the physical distribution of UPS and PLU are more significant than the number of lanes they would increase. Large sections of residential suburban housing across the region are severely underserved by public transportation, which leaves room for the universities to pedestrianize pool trips for the communities immediately surrounding. For both PLU and UPS, this might mean that a few limited hours with a membership fee would both ensure their facilities aren’t overstrained and provide funding to supplement student fees that support the pool.

Western Washington University (WWU) in Bellingham represents a moderated synthesis of the potential for universities in Seattle by increasing the lane capacity of the entire city, and in greater Tacoma, by serving as pedestrian neighborhood hubs.

Bellingham only has 16 pool lanes open to the public, and none of them are publicly owned. This means that WWU opening its pool to the public would offer the greatest relative increase in number of lanes in its community (unless we count Parkland as its own community) and provide swimming opportunities beyond the private business sector, as WWU is a public institution.

At the immediate neighborhood level, WWU’s pool opening to the public could have similar effects at pedestrianizing trips as UPS and PLU would. The main issue is that unlike the grid patterns surrounding UPS and PLU, the streets surrounding WWU are elongated with few intersections, requiring pedestrians to cut across private property for the quickest route.

The bus routes connecting to WWU also already feed into the downtown Bellingham core where pools already exist, so locals around the university would most practically cycle to the pool rather than walk or take transit. One might consider it a tertiary benefit: residents would get the benefit of a light warmup and cooldown exercise.

So what value can we attach to this contribution? Shoreline is suggesting $100 million for its new eight-lane complex with extra amenities, but this includes a non-lap pool, Jacuzzi, saunas, etc. Let’s say we say the lap pool represents a third of the value of that facility: that’s $33 million for eight lanes, a little more than $4 million per lane. As those lanes are going to be used by the public exclusively whereas university pools would require limited hours to accommodate swim teams, let’s shave that down even more to just $500,000 per lane.

At that rate, UW and Seattle U opening their pools to the public even in a limited capacity would still represent a $13 million capital improvement to the community. UPS and PLU $7 million, and WWU $3 million. This represents an extremely conservative estimate, as public pool facilities regularly cost tens of millions of dollars, and it’s all money that communities would not have to spend if these universities provided a means for the public to access their facilities even in a limited capacity that accommodates student athletics.

What about value beyond dollar figures, for those of us who aren’t neoliberal capitalists? Pools serve as a vital third space that uniquely combines relaxation and fitness to all ages and nearly all levels of ability: after work or school people can unwind in isolation by swimming laps or building community in group activities. It’s also a place to develop swimming skills which save people’s lives .

By opening their pools to the public, these universities would allow more areas to become walkable, enjoyable, and safer all while more fully integrating themselves into their surrounding communities. These are the types of broad social goals administrators at these institutions constantly profess, and they should feel fortunate that they have the opportunity to realize them so easily in this instance.

articles.title: A new climb: Capitol Hill’s Annapurna Cafe gets an early start on its plan to move up Broadway
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: For its trek to the top of Seattle process to create a new, updated home for the beloved Himalayan joint, Broadway’s Annapurna Cafe is starting early.
Late this summer, Annapurna’s owners filed permit paperwork to begin buildout on a brand new Broadway space for the restaurant — work they don’t expect to start until next November.
“We heard that the City of Seattle is really behind for improvement approval,” Sujan Sharma tells CHS about the paperwork.

While Sharma and Roshita Shrestha continue to serve their much-loved thalis, curries, and breads in its underground space below the old Crest Building at 1833 Broadway, Annapurna is being prepared for a climb north.

A few years back, Sharma and Shrestha purchased a Broadway commercial condo on the street level of the Brix building near a few doors down from Vivace . The corner was the long ago home of Dilettante Mocha Café . The couple have leased the space to Star Sushi in recent years.
Plans are now in motion for it become Annapurna’s new home.

Working with Nos Narin , the design director at Catch Design Studio behind many Capitol Hill food and drink overhauls, the space is being planned for a full upgrade including an overhaul of the kitchen, plus a redesign of the interior — once the city finally signs off on the plans over the coming months.

The new start for Annapurna will come after more than 20 years on Broadway. Shrestha and Sharma started Annapurna in May 2003 as a small venture to introduce the cuisine to Broadway and the Capitol Hill neighborhood. Shrestha said that she wanted to bring flavors that she had grown up with to Seattle. Challenges around the pandemic and the years of construction for the Capitol Hill Light Rail Station and its next door west-side entrance nearly did the restaurant in. But Annapurna persevered — and expanded. In 2015, it reached the surface on Broadway, adding its upstairs Yeti Bar above the lower level Broadway restaurant.
Any redevelopment at 1833 Broadway will need a new, landmarks-friendly design

As for the 1905-built-building the restaurant currently calls home, it has long been lined up for redevelopment as a six-story, 50-unit mixed-use building under plans first approved a decade ago . That project was put on ice due to landmarks protections . Any new development plan will need to incorporate preservation of the building’s historic proportions, look, and feel.
The extra time has given Annapurna time to prepare and, along the way, learn a few lessons about Seattle process including the most important — start early.
Annapurna Cafe is still located at 1833 Broadway. Learn more at annapurnacafe.com .

articles.title: What’s Up With the Seahawks Owners’ Weird Son and His AI Obsession?
articles.author: Matthew Roberson
paras: On September 9, the Khosla family—who got uber rich from computer stuff—was officially introduced as the new owners of the Seattle Seahawks.

At the Khoslas’ inaugural press conference at Lumen Field, billionaire venture capitalist Vinod (one of the founders of Sun Microsystems, the company that invented Java) sat between his wife, Neeru (a molecular biologist and nonprofit cofounder), and their son, Neal (himself a Silicon Valley CEO in the health care field). The family promised to take a hands-off approach to the football side of team operations, announced the return of white throwback jerseys in 2027, and effused praise on Seattle’s zealous fanbase.

It was all pretty standard stuff, especially given that their gazillion-dollar purchase (read: $9.6 billion) bought them the defending Super Bowl champions, and the Bay Area–based family was cautious not to rock the boat too much. But a few sartorial details of that afternoon hinted at a much more tech-ified existence for the Seahawks, even more so than when they were run by Microsoft pioneer Paul Allen. A boots-on-the-ground ESPN story reported that Vinod, a 71-year-old man, wore Seahawk-colored shoes designed by ChatGPT. Meanwhile, Neal, 33 years old and very online, weighed in with his own thoughts on the contentious and Earth-destroying technology. “We’re not here to make decisions about how AI gets used in football,” the Khosla son, whose official title with the Seahawks is “vice chair,” said. “I think we’re here to have those conversations and hopefully bring some new ideas.”

While some signs were there—Neal, as far as we know, did not rock a fresh pair of ChatGPT 1s, though he did sport a leather bomber jacket, the type a tech bro would wear to speak to a computer science class and definitely turn the chair around backward—Neal was quiet about how much chatbots actually rule his life. For that, we have to go to his incredibly cursed X account , which boasts 37,000 followers and greets visitors with a bio that reads, “I judge myself on what my 8 and 80 year old selves would think.” Perhaps for obvious reasons, he kept his freakazoid internet habits on the down-low while answering questions about publicly entering the jock space. But just one day before that landmark press conference—the price was the highest ever paid for an NFL franchise, and the Khoslas became the first owners of Indian descent in league history—he was posting about Ultra GPT-6 Astra, Open AI’s business-specific model. I’m not entirely sure what this image means or what Ultra GPT-6 Astra does, because I’m a person who regularly goes outside. What I do know is that Neal captioned this screenshot with a simple “fuck it we ball,” which caused every fiber of my being to simultaneously cringe.

Mere hours before that, he was touting the work of a company called Forus, quoting a post from the Forus CEO all about how they were bringing AI to the medical field, a horrifying proposition for anyone who watched Season 2 of The Pitt . “Great company. Great founder,” Khosla wrote (presumably using his own fingers, but who knows?), while someone in the comments wondered if he was part of the New World Order.

The AI posts didn’t stop there. On September 18, now with a much more visible profile after the Seahawks began their 2026 season, Khosla authored his opinion on OpenAI’s Astra being superior to Muse, the agent developed by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta. Not only that, he did so in cutesy language clearly indicative of a digital native.

Again, I’m not totally sure what any of this means, because I mostly deal in the human realm. But on September 21, Khosla posited that this current artificial intelligence hellscape is actually “the magic golden era of agents” and cryptically alluded to WalMart having something to do with it ? To his credit, Khosla does seem to possess some self-awareness about his obvious AI infatuation, taking to X on October 2 to state that he is weary of AI psychosis at Anthropic , particularly because he believes the company is building a “conscious god”, then later quoting himself with more e-girl speak: “it’s giving aztec empire.” All right, man.

I’m sure this really made waves in the light-up keyboard, multiple monitor community, as did his ensuing bars on October 3 about how “computer use is coming for phones and it’s going to be a knife fight.” Whatever you say, babe.

It wasn’t until a few days later, though, that Khosla put out his pièces de résistance . The first one—which, I will remind you, is coming from a purported computer genius who is the top-ranking official of a tech company—apologized for getting hacked. If you were duped by this hack and got involved with any sort of Neal Khosla cryptocurrency, DO NOT BUY ANYTHING!

Then, not even 48 hours after the embarrassment of his two-factor authentication failing him, Khosla decided to compound his humiliation by showing everyone that he used Fo, an AI agent from the San Francisco startup Wajo—not even one of the most well-known AI purveyors!—to execute the simple task of buying flowers for his fiancée. In this case, the AI snitched on him for using it to write a heartfelt note, because apparently “Love you. Hope you have a great week!” would have been too complicated to come up with on his own.

People made fun of him accordingly, prompting a five-part defense where he owned up to his laziness, acknowledged his fiancée was as pissed about the note as the angry mob in his mentions, and then turned the tables and asked when was the last time you bought flowers for your lover? (By the way, Khosla likes Fo because it was able to call pharmacies and inquire about his dog’s medication , a problem that Alexander Graham Bell solved in 1876.)

This daring disruptor, who theoretically has the power to decide things like how the Seahawks should handle ticket sales or if stadium employees could be replaced by robots, went dormant for a while after that. That’s nothing new for Khosla, or his company, Curai Health, which has not tweeted since 2024. Khosla’s personal website —which, like the Curai account, is linked in his bio—is strangely private and requires a special login to access, making it literally impossible to see what he’s up to on there.

But with the Seahawks getting their season back on track after a resounding primetime win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday night, he dipped his toes back in the water with a safe, uncontroversial Tuesday morning post about how there’s nothing like Lumen Field when the 12th Man is at its loudest. Then, later that day, when news broke that the Seahawks had traded for future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson, Khosla couldn’t resist firing off a doctored photo of Seattle general manager John Schneider with glowing red eyes.
This seemed to mark the end of his full digital cleanse, which included not responding to a request for comment via the Contact Us page on Curai’s website.
