articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I’m a 45-year-old single gay cis man out there in the world. I met a 50-year-old cis married man on Grindr. We had hot sex and have been hitting it off ever since. Here’s the problem: I was under the impression at first that he and his wife practiced some form of ENM or had some version of a “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” agreement. At this point, however, I know that all the man-on-man sex he’s having with me and others is just old-fashioned cheating. Among other pieces of evidence that he’s cheating: He’s having his PrEP and DoxyPEP mailed to my address (good on him for being proactive about this) and he goes out of his way to cover his tracks in other ways. More context: His spouse is the breadwinner and he stays at home. Housework is work, of course, and he does the housework, but he has no income. They’ve been married for more than 25 years and they haven’t had sex of any kind in at least eighteen years. He jokes about maybe having a sex addiction and is also a little smug about getting away with fucking whoever he wants, whenever he wants. Do you think the wife should be tipped off to what he’s doing? She is going to find out eventually… I’m certain of that. Also, he’s got a teenage son who is gay and out and he can’t seem to see the problem of his being in the closet while his son is out.
Is this guy a lost cause? Should I cut ties? Or is there a way forward?

You clearly wanna tell this guy’s wife he’s been cheating on her — I’m getting subtle “aggrieved mistress” vibes from your question — but I don’t think you’ll be telling his wife anything she doesn’t already know. She may not know her husband is bisexual and fucking you and God only knows how many other men, CHEAT, but she most likely assumes he hasn’t been celibate for the last eighteen years.

That said, being confronted with the proof — of his cheating and his bisexuality — could cause this woman pain, CHEAT. For all you know, he’s the reason their marriage is sexless and she has lived every day for nearly two decades with the sting of her husband’s sexual rejection. So, why does she stay? Well, sometimes a person is able to limp along in a sexless marriage because they believe the sexual deprivation is mutual — they believe this misery is a load they share — but finding out your spouse is out there taking loads while you read the books and make the appointments … yeah, this guy’s wife could go from resigned and content to wounded and devastated before she finishes reading your email.

But maybe everything this guy has told you about his marriage is true — always a big leap when a married person wants to get into your pants — and his wife is one of those women who doesn’t wanna fuck her husband but won’t give her husband permission to fuck anyone else. If that’s the case, then your lover is only guilty of doing what he needs to do to stay married and stay sane. And if there are good reasons why they stay together — financial dependence is one reason people stay, CHEAT, but so is emotional/social dependence — then your email could wind up doing more harm than good.

Look, you’re free to find it sad that this man isn’t out to his wife or his gay kid, CHEAT, but I don’t think you have a right to blow up his life — his thoroughly compromised life — because you think it would be better for all involved (presumably yourself included) if he was out. It sounds like this guy is a bit of an asshole… and it sounds like you caught feelings for him at some point… and now you feel like you’ve been used. But outing a cheater for cheating when you’re done cheating with him (or he’s done cheating with you) is always a bad look.
P.S. If the “way forward” you’re imagining is some sort of future where you’re with this guy… yeah, maybe you tell him what you’re feeling instead of telling his wife what he’s been doing.

I am a 40-year-old cisgender bi woman living in the Midwest. I have a question about one of my best friends, a trans woman. I’ve known this person for over fifteen years, most of that before their transition. They grew up as a white man, middle class, and didn’t deal with any of the things that women deal with growing up. I’m referencing harassment and assault, especially with the recent case in the news of the students at Cornell University. This individual grew up to be a relatively successful man with a six-figure income, nice house, and a pretty average life. They came out as trans a few years ago and I’ve been incredibly supportive during their transition. The thing that I’m having trouble with is their newfound “feminism.” When we talk about the struggles women face, they speak as someone who has been through and lived through those experiences. As an AFAB woman who grew up in the 1990s and 2000s and has dealt with harassment and sexual assault, this is really upsetting to me. I absolutely love my friend, but it really hurts me when they claim to understand the plight of women in America when they have identified as a woman for less than three years. How can I bring this topic up without turning it into a major argument? Am I being too sensitive? Should I just agree with them and move on? I need help here.

I’m not a woman, TRA, but I do listen to women (when I remember to close my mouth) and I try not to talk over women (which is easier to do with my mouth closed). I like to think that all that listening has given me — a cis man — some understanding, however imperfect and incomplete, of what women face. So, it’s possible your friend… if she was listening before her transition… has some understanding herself.
But your annoyance with your friend, this recently hatched egg , is likewise understandable.

I’ve been out and gay for — OMG — more than forty years, TRA, and nothing annoys me more than having gayness explained to me by someone who has been out and gay for forty minutes. In some cases, these newly out guys are being thoughtless. But in others, TRA, the newly out guy isn’t talking to me. They’re not saying things I need to hear… they’re saying things they need to hear. But my M.O. is the same in both cases: I let them talk. Even if it means having to listen to someone who was born in 2002 explain to me just how bad things were for gay people in the 1980s, I let them talk. They either realize they’re being ridiculous (“I mean, I don’t need to tell you this!”) or they hear what they needed to hear and the conversation moves on to other things. (I do reserve the right to blow up when a newly out cis gay man tries to tell me that cis gay men played no role in the struggle for gay rights — we just partied, fucked, and died while nonbinary asexuals did the heavy lifting — or that the gay rights movement was hijacked in the 1990s by gay men who wanted to throw themselves wedding showers. Those are fighting words.)

So, my advice: Let your old friend run her mouth. Don’t argue, stare blankly, and change the subject when there’s a lull. Here’s hoping your friend, like those newly out gay boys, eventually gets this shit out of her system. But if she doesn’t — if she literally can’t stop explaining womanhood to you — feel free to spend less time with her.

articles.title: Inside the Gremlins Museum
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: “Where can I get a Gremlin?” was the question Ian Grant asked himself when he first saw the comedy-horror Christmas film at the drive-in back in 1984. “I was probably too young to see it,” he admitted. Although the film fueled nightmares of little green monsters under his bed, it also sparked a lifelong obsession (love and fear are closely related, after all).

It took nearly four decades for Grant to make his childhood dream a reality. He acquired a rare gremlin puppet from the first movie on eBay, and it was in rough condition—typical for other 35-year-old puppets. Grant worked with foam-latex restoration artists to repair his treasured prop back to form, while preserving its original elements. This was the start of the Gremlins Museum—a quaint office and hallway in Grant’s home—which now displays dozens of original props, puppets, scripts, and posters from Gremlins and Gremlins 2: The New Batch , as well as hundreds of pieces of merchandise from both films.

The giant screen-used Gizmo immediately took our breath away when we walked into the room. Crafted for the sequel , this large-scale animatronic puppet was used for close-up shots in the film and reportedly cost approximately $250,000 to produce. While as many as 20 little Gizmo puppets were created for the film, only one giant Gizmo (or as Grant calls it, the “hero puppet”) was made. “When I first got him, he kinda had a deer-in-headlights look to him,” Grant recalled. But during the restoration process, his wide-eyed facial expression was adjusted to make him look calmer, sweeter, and more like himself.

Beside the giant Gizmo are his normal-scale animatronic Mogwai buddies from Gremlins 2, including Mohawk, George, and Daffy. It can’t be overstated just how soft these guys looked. We asked repeatedly if Grant ever gives his puppets a pat on the head or a belly rub, but he stressed that they were far too fragile. However, he did confirm that Daffy was just as soft as he looks: “I had to touch him a little bit extra to get him situated on his stand.”
Owning and restoring these pieces of film history is a big job. These puppets were not made to last, and Grant reveals that if they are not maintained, they will essentially turn to dust.

“Everybody that owns foam latex stuff has this nightmare of waking up to foam dust everywhere,” he said as we gasped in horror. All the puppets at the Gremlins Museum are showcased and preserved in museum-quality glass boxes. “This is their safe place,” says Grant. “Nobody can hurt them in the box.”

Facing the Mogwai is Grant’s collection of Gremlins. He owns three gremlin puppets from the first movie and an original sculpt, which was used to create the puppets. While the Gremlins in the first film are fairly generic creatures, the sequel is a different story (perhaps you know, if you’ve seen the Key & Peele sketch ). The Gremlins in The New Batch are unique little monsters with names, personalities, and special abilities. Grant’s collection includes Bat Gremlin, Vegetable Gremlin, Lenny Gremlin, George Gremlin, Phantom Gremlin, “Out of Ammo” Gremlin (who shoots at John Wayne in a western scene which appears in an alternate VHS cut of the film), and most importantly, Greta Gremlin (aka the Girl Gremlin). Grant owns the “hero puppet” of Greta, meaning she was a functional animatronic and used in most of the movie scenes, as well as the sexy press pics. Grant notes that his puppet is the one used in the “iconic hand-on-hip” photo, which I, as a Greta stan, of course knew what photo he was talking about.

Other props in the museum include Gizmo’s pink Corvette, a Gremlin-used chainsaw, and a tiny gun (fired by a bandit Gremlin), all of which were used in the first film. Grant has acquired most of his props and puppets by becoming friends with folks who worked on the film and negotiating sales before they go on official auction markets. He noted that auctions are a losing game, considering that fees are high and that “there will always be someone with more money than you.” One of whom is Lord of the Rings director Peter Jackson, who is apparently also a Gremlins prop collector. “There was a big auction in 2022, and I went in hoping to get a bunch of stuff, but he came in and just killed everybody. I can’t compete with a billionaire.”

Since the museum is in Grant’s home, it is not open to the general public, but he welcomes a handful of passionate fans and media inquirers to take a peek at his collection. He also runs an extremely detailed online archive with virtual tours of the collection so that the creatures can be enjoyed by all. As of now, he has no current plans to expand the museum, but has considered contacting the Museum of Pop Culture to display the collection to the masses. However, the transportation of these fragile artifacts is a cause for concern. “It’s literally my nightmare…” he said with a laugh.

articles.title: How the Crosslake Connection Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On March 28, Sound Transit opened the much anticipated Crosslake Connection. This rail connection between Seattle and cities on the Eastside promised fast, frequent, and more reliable connectivity across Lake Washington. The Link 2 Line was designed to replace the hundreds of daily bus trips on I-90, freeing up service hours to improve local bus routes. Initially, however, the I-90 bus routes remained intact to offer extra capacity and redundancy during the World Cup. In the five months following the Crosslake Connection opening, passengers could either take the train or bus. Many chose to take the train. In August 2026, the 11 Link stations on the Eastside and Mercer Island accounted for 12,500 boardings each weekday.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in east King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.
Sound Transit Express routes 550 and 554 provided all-day bus service across Lake Washington via I-90. Following the full 2 Line opening, many people switched from one of these routes to Link.

Overall ridership on Route 550 dropped 52% year-over-year. Boardings at the route’s busiest stop in 2025, Bellevue Transit Center, fell 57% as many passengers opted to take the 2 Line instead. Along Bellevue Way, the stop at 4th Street took the crown as the busiest stop with 278 weekday boardings (this stop had 366 weekday boardings in 2025). The other stops on Bellevue Way did not see significant changes in ridership. One stop that saw an increase in passenger boardings is South Bellevue station for Bellevue-bound trips. Passengers transferring from the 2 Line to Route 550 to access a stop on Bellevue Way doubled the boarding count to 50 per day. Route 550 stops near South Bellevue station and Mercer Island station. Seattle-bound boardings on Route 550 at those stops dropped by 78% and 74%, respectively.

Similar to Route 550, ridership on Route 554 fell where it overlaps with Link but remained constant elsewhere. Route 554’s stops in Issaquah had similar ridership to 2025. However, boardings at the Eastgate P&R (I-90 & 142nd Pl) fell 42%. This is likely due to more people choosing to use the nearby South Bellevue P&R and Link instead. On Mercer Island, the number of passengers boarding a Route 554 bus dropped 72% as many switched to the 2 Line. Route 554 was replaced by Route 556 in August. Route 556 provides more frequent service between Issaquah and Bellevue, via South Bellevue station and Bellevue Way.

State Route 520 is the only other connection between Seattle and the Eastside across Lake Washington. Some bus routes that use SR-520, such as Route 255, do not complete with the 2 Line and saw negligible changes in ridership patterns following the 2 Line opening. Other routes had significant changes as some passengers switched to the Link 2 Line.

While Route 545 takes a different route from Link across Lake Washington, it offers redundant service with the 2 Line between Redmond and downtown Seattle. Following the full 2 Line opening, ridership on the route fell 20%. At SR-520 & 40th St (near Redmond Technology station), inbound boardings fell 19%. Likewise, boardings at Redmond Transit Center dropped by 23%.

In downtown Seattle, Route 545 ridership has shifted north. Stops along Olive Way had a collective 2.5% increase in boardings, despite the closure of the peak-only stop at Boren Ave. Meanwhile, stops on 4th Ave had a collective 36% decrease in passenger boardings. This reflects passengers choosing to take the fastest trip. Route 545 is often faster than Link between the Denny Triangle and Redmond, while Link is usually faster between Redmond and CID or Pioneer Square. After all, Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think .

Compared to the 2 Line, Route 542 offers a shortcut between Redmond and the U District. A trip from the U District to downtown Redmond on Link takes 56 minutes vs just 32 minutes via Route 542. Ridership on this route has remained steady, with a 2.4% increase in boardings year-over-year. There were no significant changes to the route’s ridership patterns.

Route 271 also connected Seattle with the Eastside via SR-520. The long route had several noticeable changes in its ridership patterns following the opening of the Crosslake Connection. Trips between the U District and downtown Bellevue take 37 minutes on Link vs 24 minutes on Route 271. Despite the faster trip time on Route 271, the number of passengers boarding Seattle-bound trips at Bellevue Transit Center dropped 47%. This is likely from passengers who previously connected to another route in the U District and now have a more time-competitive option with Link (eg: trips from Bellevue to Capitol Hill).
Route 271 also had a 41% decrease in boardings at Eastgate Park & Ride. This is the same changed observed with Route 554 and is likely to due more people using the South Bellevue P&R instead.

The only new 2 Line station in Seattle, Judkins Park, impacted the ridership patterns of the five King County Metro routes that stop nearby: routes 7, 8, 9, 48, and 106. The intersection of an east-west Link station and five north-south bus routes is a key opportunity for many transfers. However, the data show that only 486 people are transferring between Link and one of the bus routes each weekday. This accounts for about ⅓ of boardings at Judkins Park station, a bit less than the projected 42% . The table below breaks down the bus boardings at Judkins Park station by route and direction.

The Crosslake Connection is already making its mark on travel patterns across Lake Washington. Many passengers switched from routes 271, 545, 550, and 554 to Link when it was the faster option. In Seattle, fewer people than expected are transferring between buses and the 2 Line at Judkins Park station.

The five month period of overlapping Link and bus service has come to a close and many bus routes were truncated in August . Seattle Transit Blog will share ridership data analysis from those changes in Spring 2027 (when the data are available).

In the meantime, explore detailed ridership data for most King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Community Transit routes at seattletransitridership.com . The dashboard has been updated to include stop-level data for all Metro and Metro operated Sound Transit routes from the Spring 2026 service change. The impact of the Federal Way Link Extension on bus routes in south King County will be discussed in an article tomorrow.

articles.title: Most Puget Sound Cities Aren't Keeping Up With Housing Growth Targets
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A small number of cities across central Puget Sound are pulling along the entire region when it comes to keeping pace with long-term housing growth targets, according to new data released by the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC). Of the 40 cities across King, Pierce, Snohomish and Kitsap Counties that are expected to accommodate the largest share of regional housing growth through 2044, just 14 are on track and many are significantly behind.

The data provides a snapshot of uneven urban growth, more than a half-decade after a pivot in the four-county region's housing growth strategy toward transit investments that were either already in place or coming online. Though that strategy is clearly bearing some fruit, with cities like Shoreline, Redmond, and Mountlake Terrace easily dispatching with their targets, these numbers also point to the need for potential reforms around land use and building regulations elsewhere – some of which are already in motion.

"The region is producing housing at pace to meet its targets, but this is largely led by just a handful of jurisdictions," Eric Clute, a planner in PSRC's data department, said last week while breaking down the data for local elected officials. "I think these jurisdictions can offer a blueprint to others looking to boost production and meet their housing targets."

The adopted growth targets on the books right now across the urban areas of all four counties plan for a total of approximately 620,000 new units of housing by 2044, with close to half of that in King County. As a whole, the region has been outpacing that target, adding around 183,000 units since 2019 or 2020 – the start year varies by county, with the clock starting for King County in 2019, compared to 2020 for the other three counties.

That growth rate is around 16,000 more units than was needed to keep pace. But without growth in Seattle significantly outpacing its growth target – 70,000 units were built compared to a prorated growth target of just over 31,000 – the region as a whole would not be ahead of the overall target. Falling short will mean that Washington will likely fail to add the 1.1 million overall homes needed over the next two decades to tread water on housing affordability, according to the state's Commerce Department.

PSRC's Vision 2050 growth strategy lays out different tiers of jurisdictions expected to shoulder decreasing shares of regional housing growth. At the top are the metro cities, including Seattle, Tacoma, Bellevue, Everett, and Bremerton. These cities have the biggest growth targets, though a smaller overall target for Kitsap County means some cities across the Sound are aiming for more housing than Bremerton.

Out of those five, only Seattle outpaced its growth target, with Everett lagging the most. Snohomish County's largest city logged just over 2,000 new homes compared to an overall target of 36,500 by 2044. Bellevue did better , seeing more than 5,000 units built against a similar target. Tacoma saw more than 7,000 new units, but has an even more ambitious growth target of 43,000.

Just below those five big kahunas are the "core cities," mid-sized jurisdictions that are also expected to carry a significant amount of regional growth. Just four out of 15 of those cities – Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah and Kent – are meeting or exceeding their targets. Renton, Auburn and Federal are falling the furthest short, while Lynnwood and Bothell are doing better.

Outside of metro and core cities, another set of cities known as "high capacity transit (HCT) communities" are also planning for a fairly significant share of growth. HCT communities feature some type of current or future transit investments, from a Sounder commuter or Link light rail station to a planned bus rapid transit line.

Nine of those 20 cities are on track, with Shoreline leading the pack. Woodinville, Mountlake Terrace, and Port Orchard are other standouts here, with Edmonds falling significantly short of expectations. DuPont, which had been set to see an extension of Sound Transit's S Line until an agency board vote earlier this year through a construction timeline into limbo , saw essentially no housing growth at all.

The good news here is that required updates to local growth plans made by the end of 2024, along with required zoning adjustments to allow more types of housing in lower density neighborhoods the following year, are just starting to bear fruit. In the metro cities specifically, many of those adjustments were bold ones, including the Home in Tacoma rezones and Bellevue's land use code reforms that targeted areas ripe for redevelopment, like Wilburton .

"We have all made recent updates to Comprehensive Plans that made significant changes to spur housing production," Clute said. "These changes are likely not yet showing up in the data. Those changes were done just a couple years ago, or a year ago, and development takes several years to happen."

And then there are the cities and towns that are not expected to shoulder as much growth, places like North Bend, Gig Harbor, and Lake Stevens. Growth in those places, on the whole, has been significantly outpacing growth targets, a fact that stands in stark contrast with the bigger cities that are lagging behind.

What about urban unincorporated areas? Areas outside cities and towns but still inside the urban growth area (UGA) saw significant growth in Pierce County, and less growth in Snohomish and Kitsap Counties. King County's modest urban unincorporated growth target is right on pace.

Slower-than-expected growth in unincorporated Kitsap County is likely good news for urbanists, who have argued that the growth plans for those areas set up suburban sprawl . On the other hand, unincorporated Snohomish County includes areas set to see light rail expansion, including the vicinity of the Ash Way and Mariner Park and Ride stations being built as part of Everett Link .

Ultimately, the numbers released last week could represent a new baseline, with housing production in Seattle slowing significantly and overhauled zoning across Puget Sound potentially setting the stage for increased growth elsewhere. If Seattle's steady homebuilding pace falters without other cities picking up the slack, the region could be in for more housing affordability woes.

While underlying land use regulations clearly aren't the only factor at play when it comes to regional growth, they do play a big role. And though the region as a whole may be slightly ahead of the curve, that's no reason for any city to sit on its laurels.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Vote Yes on Prop 1 for More Buses!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Ballots for the November election have been sent to voters in King County. One item on the ballot for voters in Seattle is Proposition 1: Seattle Transit Measure. This renews and expands the Seattle Transit Measure that is set to expire in early 2027. The 0.3% sales tax is expected to generate $138 million per year that will fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years, 100,000 more bus trips than currently funded. It would also fund 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. Vote Yes to help fund transit in Seattle.

Since 2014, the Seattle Transit Measure has funded millions of bus trips in Seattle. Many of these trips are on weekends when most routes have less frequent service compared to weekdays. Route 36 is one such route that has received additional weekend trips. Between 2022 and 2026, the STM funded 22 additional trips on Saturdays and 42 additional trips on Sunday. In response, more people use Route 36 every weekend. Compared to 2022, Route 36 ridership on Saturday and Sunday has increased by 41% and 58%, respectively. Weekday ridership has increased 32%. This increased ridership represents more car-free trips and improved access to get to work, shops, and fun for people in Beacon Hill, Othello, and the International District.

The Route 36 success story is not an isolated one. Passengers on routes around Seatttle have benefited from additional service funded by the Seattle Transit Measure. Vote Yes to continue and expand the additional bus trips. Fill out your ballot soon and drop it off at one of the many ballot drop boxes in King County.

articles.title: Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: Much like route 550 was to Bellevue, route 545 has been Redmond’s workhorse route. Redmond has a diverse set of transit options fanning out in every direction, even before it had the distinction of being a Link terminus. But the main regional service has always been route 545, which connects downtown Redmond to downtown Seattle. However, as with many ST express corridors, route 545 was intended to be an interim service until rail reaches Redmond. Route 545 was always planned on being discontinued with the start of East Link service to Seattle, with the 2 Line taking over the entirety of both routes 545 and 550. The original plan (developed as part of the first iteration of King County Metro’s East Link Connections plan) deleted the 545 and 550, with some of the freed up service hours being used to make the 542 frequent and replace 545 service to Bear Creek P&R. Route 554 (later renumbered 556) was also planned to be moved to Bellevue to fill a gap in service on Bellevue Way left by the removal of route 550. Former riders of these routes either take a more frequent bus to connect the 2 Line, or can just take the 2 Line on its own.

Sound transit first let riders formally have a say on the potential changes in early 2025 as part of their 2026 service plan, and have a say they did! They received more feedback on route 545 than any other route by far, with its feedback results showing about 14% of respondents providing feedback on route 545, the runner-up being route 550 with about 9%. The broad consensus of the feedback was clear: don’t delete route 545. Sound Transit was so moved by these results that they did not even propose any changes to route 545 at all in any of their own ST Express proposals, even while moving forward with major changes nearby such as deleting route 550 and combining route 554 with route 556, relying entirely on Link to get I-90 riders to Seattle.

The reasoning is sensible. The 2 Line crosses the lake along I-90, so buses heading to Seattle via I-90 are the most duplicative of rail, and forcing a transfer would add little travel time (or even save time in some cases). Route 545, on the other hand, has a straight shot to downtown Seattle via the 520 bridge. Trading that for a detour to I-90 through Bellevue would add travel time, and riders told Sound Transit that this additional travel time isn’t acceptable. So when planning the 2026 ST Express network, Sound Transit decided to keep buses when travel times by cutting them would exceed 10 minutes (per The Urbanist , reporting from Sound Transit’s Director of System and Service Planning, Emily Yasukochi).

In keeping with the feedback they received, Sound Transit’s eventual plan had routes 545 and 542 in the “no changes” column. Here are the resulting service frequencies as they took effect late last month:

During the week, riders will continue to have frequent service on route 545, but riders heading to UW or farther north opting to use the 542 will have no frequent service at any time. Missing a 542 could make taking the 2 Line all the around through Bellevue, Mercer Island, and downtown Seattle be a faster way to get to UW just because of the 30 minute wait. Worse yet, neither the 542 or 545 are frequent on weekends, making riders who have a faster trip have to decide between a fast but infrequent bus, or a frequent but circuitous train. By comparison, route 556 (which replaces route 554 and connects Issaquah to the 2 Line) sees frequent service every day of the week, and is also more usable for intra-eastside trips (e.g., Issaquah to Bellevue or Redmond) than route 554 was.

As part of its reporting on its proposals in the 2026 service plan, Sound Transit did an analysis of travel times on routes which were to be modified in 2026. Below is its analysis, which includes some popular trips which were made on routes 522, 550, 554, 556, 574, and 586 before the 2026 changes. They estimated travel times on these trips before the 2026 service changes (labeled “current”), and did the same estimate for travel times after the service changes (labeled “future”), under the new network. The final column gives an estimated additional travel time for each trip after the 2026 changes, with negative values indicating a quicker trip.
Per the rest of the document, these estimates are calculated by adding:

With Sound Transit being selective about which changes were made, it’s unsurprising that most of these trips saw a travel time decrease, with only Issaquah TC- downtown Seattle being slower in every case. More to the point, in all cases but one, additional travel time is less than the 10 minute threshold Sound Transit set for planning bus changes to new Link service.

Because Sound Transit did not make changes to route 545, they did not provide their travel time analysis. I suspect they analyzed trips on route 545 against the same trips on the Link 2 Line, as all trips between Redmond and Seattle on routes 545 map decently well to a single 2 Line trip. However, assuming route 545 is cut and service is added to route 542 (as proposed in 2021), a frequent route 542 with a transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW could also approximate any route 545 trip. Below is an analysis I did of six trips on route 545, using the same method Sound Transit used to calculate the other changes:

Trip A: Downtown Redmond to International District/Chinatown Station Trip B: Downtown Redmond to Westlake Station Trip C: Redmond Technology Station to International District/Chinatown Station Trip D: Redmond Technology Station to Westlake Station Trip E: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to International District/Chinatown Station Trip F: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to Westlake Station

To easily see the impact of the changes, I’ve colored cells red if times are more than 10 minutes longer, green if more than 5 minutes shorter, a shade of yellow if less than 10 minutes longer, and a shade of blue of less than 5 minutes shorter. I’ve also marked 2 Line-only travel times in italics , and 542 + 1/2 Line travel times in bold .

From the results, I think Sound Transit only analyzed the travel time impact of 2 Line-only trips, and did not consider 542 + 1/2 Line at all. Because while (to my surprise) the 2 Line competes with route 545 very well on most trips, the directness of route 545 to Redmond Technology Station makes those trips impossible to match on the 2 Line, with an added delay of 20 minutes in the worst case. But when you add in the option to take the more frequent 542 and transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW, this adds a faster option in the exact cases where the single 2 Line trip fares the worst against the 545. In fact, when this option is added, every case has an alternative to its route 545 trip that adds less delay than the 10 minute planning threshold Sound Transit uses, with most trips getting faster (with the most improved trip being 25 minutes faster from Marymoor to IDS).

Lastly, one thing this analysis doesn’t account for is something that you often see on route 545 toward Seattle on weekday afternoons, which are catastrophic delays. In particular, the turn from Stewart St to 5th Ave often gets so congested that route 545 buses often wait 10-20 minutes just to make this one turn. If the travel time analysis of alternative options wasn’t reason enough to move route 545 service hours elsewhere, the fact that Sound Transit is predictably wasting a large amount of service hours just waiting for this one turn just underscores how route 545 needs a second look.

If route 545 were to be deleted, this would free up a ton of service hours. Obviously the first priority would be to boost route 542 frequencies to 10 minutes peak/15 minutes midday, and extend it to Bear Creek P&R via Downtown Redmond Station (taking over the 545’s eastern section). I also think route 542 should be increased to every 15 minutes on weekends as well (something which actually wasn’t proposed in 2021 , as it kept the 542 every 30 minutes on weekends). Since half of this route 542 service already exist, this would only use up significantly less than half of route 545’s service hours.

The next priority could be restoring route 544 to South Lake Union. This was a route that Sound Transit created in March 2020 following a restructure that consolidated some service from Kirkland and Redmond to create a new route serving an emerging market for commuter service to SLU. However, being started at the beginning of the pandemic, it only operated a couple weeks before it was suspended . Originally, it proposed to be restored in 2021 as part of East Link Connections. I think this is a good idea, though I also think some changes should be made. King County Metro has shown it can run buses from SR 520 to the Mercer St exit today (something which was long though to be impossible in regular service) on route 256. Furthermore, WSDOT is planning to open a direct express lane connection between this exit and SR 520 for transit in the 2030s. So I think a restored 544 should exit at Mercer St, and could lay over at the bus layover area on Eastlake.

On the eastside, it’s also worth reevaluating whether it makes sense to run the 544 to the Overlake P&R, or even to Redmond at all. If a shorter route 544 could be made more frequent, it could facilitate 2-seat rides if moved to the right places. The way I think it could maximize connection opportunities is to serve S. Kirkland P&R, then terminate at Spring District Station, with frequencies of 8 minutes. This allows connections from routes 542 and 270 at the 520 freeway stations, some Kirkland routes at S. Kirkland, and the 2 Line at Spring District (and transfers would work well from both the east and south here).

Whether the remaining service hours after changes to the 542 go into restoring route 544 or something else entirely, what will be the case is that, while not every rider will have a faster trip, many riders will, and all riders will enjoy more frequent and consistent service across every day of the week. When express buses complement rail rather than competing with it, then both services will work better for more riders.

articles.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
articles.author: Lizz Giordano
paras: Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.
As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.
The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.
“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.
In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
